#109. Best Day Trips from Toronto: Easy Escapes for 2026

📅 14 Jul 2026 • ⏱️ 17 min read (3440 words)
General 🌐 Theplanetd

Best Day Trips from Toronto: Easy Escapes for 2026

📅 14 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read | Source: Theplanetd

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Looking for the best day trips from Toronto?
  • Industry observers note that we’ve lived in Toronto and traveled all around the province—and trust us, you don’t need to go far to find adventure.
  • Sources indicate that most of these destinations are within a 2-hour drive from Toronto, so you can head out in the morning and be back home in time for dinner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Looking for the best day trips from Toronto? Whether you’re craving waterfalls, wineries, beaches, or small towns, Ontario is packed with incredible places to explore just a short drive from the city. The best day trips from Toronto include Niagara Falls, Elora, Blue Mountain, and Prince Edward County, all within 2 to 3 hours from the city.

Industry observers note that we’ve lived in Toronto and traveled all around the province—and trust us, you don’t need to go far to find adventure. From hiking trails along the Niagara Escarpment to paddling the Grand River or sipping wine in Prince Edward County, there’s a day trip here for everyone.

Sources indicate that most of these destinations are within a 2-hour drive from Toronto, so you can head out in the morning and be back home in time for dinner. If you’re short on time but substantial on wanderlust, these are the top 25 Toronto day trips to add to your weekend plans in Ontario.

The best day trips from Toronto include Niagara Falls for first-time visitors, Hamilton for waterfalls and food, Elora for small-town charm and the gorge, Stratford for theatre, Blue Mountain for outdoor adventure, Prince Edward County for wineries and beaches, and the Toronto Islands for an easy car-free escape. Most are within 1 to 2.5 hours of the city, but places like Algonquin Park and Bruce Peninsula are better as long day trips or overnight getaways.

Hamilton is one of the best day trips from Toronto because it combines history, nature, food, art, and outdoor adventure in one easy-to-reach city.

The best day trips from Toronto include popular destinations like Niagara Falls, Hamilton, Elora, and Prince Edward County, all within 2 to 3 hours of the city.Toronto Islands and Canada’s Wonderland offer easy escapes under an hour, perfect for families and low-stress outings.Elora and Stratford are ideal for those seeking small-town charm combined with nature and culture.Longer trips such as Muskoka and Algonquin Provincial Park provide stunning wilderness experiences but require more travel time.

Best for: skyline views, beaches, biking, picnics, and car-free exploringTravel time from Toronto: 10–15 minute ferry from downtownSuggested day: Take the ferry in the morning, explore Ward’s Island or Centre Island, rent bikes, have a picnic, and return near sunset for skyline views.

The Toronto Islands are the easiest day trip from Toronto because you don’t even need to leave the city. Once you step off the ferry, it feels like a completely different world, with beaches, bike paths, picnic areas, and one of the best views of the Toronto skyline.

This is a great option if you want a low-stress day trip without a long drive. You can spend the day walking, cycling, swimming in summer, or simply relaxing by the water.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Go late afternoon if you want the best skyline photos. The view of downtown Toronto from the islands is one of the classic shots of the city.

Best for: families, thrill rides, water park fun, and summer day tripsDrive from Toronto: about 30–45 minutesSuggested day: Arrive early, hit the massive roller coasters first, cool off at Splash Works in the afternoon, and stay into the evening if the park has special events.

Industry observers note that canada’s Wonderland is one of the easiest family day trips from Toronto. It has roller coasters, kids’ areas, live entertainment, water rides, and Splash Works, which is perfect on a hot summer day.

Industry observers note that this is a full-day outing, especially if you are visiting with kids or trying to ride the major coasters. It’s busy in summer, but that is part of the experience.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Buy tickets online and arrive before opening if you want to make the most of the day. The biggest rides get long lines swiftly.

Best for: hiking, conservation areas, mountain biking, skiing, and quick nature escapesDrive from Toronto: about 40–60 minutesSuggested day: Start with a hike at Rattlesnake Point or Kelso, have lunch in town, then add Mount Nemo or Crawford Lake if you want a second outdoor stop.

Milton is one of the best quick nature escapes from Toronto. It sits along the Niagara Escarpment and gives you access to hiking trails, lookout points, conservation areas, and outdoor activities without committing to a long drive.

Kelso Conservation Area is great year-round, with hiking and mountain biking in warm weather and skiing or snowboarding in winter. Rattlesnake Point and Mount Nemo are also excellent for escarpment views.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Milton is ideal when you want a real outdoor day but don’t want to spend half the day in the car.

Best for: waterfalls, hiking, food, art, museums, and waterfront trailsDrive from Toronto: about 1 hourSuggested day: Visit a waterfall in the morning, explore Dundurn Castle or the waterfront in the afternoon, then head to James Street North for dinner or Art Crawl if it’s the second Friday of the month.

Hamilton is one of the best day trips from Toronto because it combines nature and city energy in one easy trip. You can hike to waterfalls, visit museums, walk the waterfront, eat downtown, and still be back in Toronto by evening.

Sources indicate that the waterfalls are the main draw, but Hamilton has become much more than an outdoor stop. James Street North, King William Street, the waterfront, and the city’s food scene make it worth a full day.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: If you want the full city-and-nature experience, see our guide to the best things to do in Hamilton, Ontario.

Best for: scenic drives, hiking, fall colours, cider, and countryside escapesDrive from Toronto: about 45–60 minutesSuggested day: Visit the Cheltenham Badlands, go for a hike, stop at a cidery or café, and enjoy a relaxed countryside drive.

Industry observers note that caledon is a great day trip when you want fresh air, rolling hills, and a slower pace. It’s close to Toronto but feels rural, making it perfect for a scenic drive or a low-key outdoor day.

The Cheltenham Badlands are the most famous stop, but Caledon also has trails, conservation areas, farm shops, and cideries that make it easy to turn a short drive into a full afternoon.

Recent findings suggest that dave & Deb’s Tip: Caledon is especially beautiful in fall. Go early if you are visiting popular spots during peak colour season.

Best for: first-time visitors, waterfalls, wineries, romance, and classic Ontario sightseeingDrive from Toronto: about 1.5 to 2 hoursSuggested day: Visit Niagara Falls in the morning, then drive 20 minutes to Niagara-on-the-Lake for wineries, heritage streets, boutique shopping, or dinner.

Niagara Falls is one of the most famous day trips from Toronto, and it still delivers every time. Start with Horseshoe Falls, then add Journey Behind the Falls, the Niagara SkyWheel, Clifton Hill, or the Hornblower boat cruise if you want the full experience.

According to recent reports, after the falls, slow the pace down in Niagara-on-the-Lake. The town is known for wineries, pretty streets, historic buildings, theatres, and one of the most charming main streets in Ontario.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: If it is your first visit, do the falls first while you still have energy, then end the day with wine country and dinner in Niagara-on-the-Lake.

Things to do in Niagara Falls Where to Stay in Niagara FallsNiagara on the Lake Day Tours Niagara Day Tours from TorontoNiagara on the Lake.

Best for: small-town charm, gorge views, tubing, kayaking, boutiques, and river adventuresDrive from Toronto: about 1.5 hoursSuggested day: Walk the town in the morning, hike along the Elora Gorge, have lunch downtown, then go tubing or kayaking if you are visiting in summer.

Elora is one of Ontario’s prettiest small towns and one of the best day trips from Toronto for people who want both nature and charm. The town has boutiques, bakeries, cafés, stone buildings, and a relaxed weekend feel.

The Elora Gorge is the highlight. The cliffs rise above the Grand River, and the trails offer beautiful views. In summer, tubing and kayaking add a little adventure to the day.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Elora gets busy on summer weekends, so arrive early if you want parking, lunch, and time on the river.

Best for: theatre, food, culture, gardens, romantic day trips, and small-town charmDrive from Toronto: about 2 hoursSuggested day: Explore downtown, walk along the Avon River, have lunch, browse the shops, and see a Stratford Festival performance if one fits your schedule.

Stratford is one of the best cultural day trips from Toronto. It’s known for the Stratford Festival, but even without a show, the town is worth visiting for its riverfront, restaurants, gardens, heritage buildings, and independent shops.

This is a slower, more polished day trip. It’s ideal for couples, theatre lovers, and anyone who wants a break from the city without heading into the wilderness.

Sources indicate that dave & Deb’s Tip: If you are seeing a show, build extra time into the day. Stratford is made for wandering before or after the theatre.

Best for: small towns, paddling, biking, river views, history, and easy food stopsDrive from Toronto: about 1.5 hoursSuggested day: Start in Paris for river views, shops, and lunch, then continue to Brantford for the Bell Homestead, Grand River trails, or a bike ride.

Paris is one of the prettiest small towns in Ontario, with the Grand River running through town, a compact downtown, cafés, bakeries, and great views from the riverfront. It’s a perfect low-key day trip when you want somewhere pretty but not overcomplicated.

Sources indicate that nearby Brantford adds history and trails to the day. The Bell Homestead tells the story of Alexander Graham Bell and the first long-distance telephone call, while the Grand River trails are excellent for walking, biking, and paddling.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Pairing Paris and Brantford makes the day feel more complete. Do Paris for the charm and Brantford for the history and trails.

Best for: markets, food, Mennonite culture, tech-meets-tradition, families, and easy wanderingDrive from Toronto: about 1.5 hoursSuggested day: Visit St. Jacobs Farmers’ Market in the morning, explore the village, then head into Kitchener-Waterloo or Cambridge for food, history, or the Butterfly Conservatory.

Kitchener-Waterloo and St. Jacobs make a great day trip because they offer such a mix of experiences. You can visit one of the best-known markets in Ontario, see Mennonite farms and horse-drawn buggies, then head into a modern university and tech region.

St. Jacobs is the classic stop, especially if you love markets, bakeries, crafts, and small-town shopping. Nearby Kitchener, Waterloo, Cambridge, and Galt add more food, history, and riverside exploring.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Go on a market day if you can. St. Jacobs Farmers’ Market is the anchor of this day trip.

Best for: beach-town nostalgia, Lake Erie, fish and chips, pier walks, and casual summer daysDrive from Toronto: about 2 hoursSuggested day: Walk the pier, have lunch at The Arbor or a local fish-and-chips spot, relax by the beach, then continue along Lake Erie if you want a mini road trip.

Industry observers note that port Dover is a classic Ontario beach town. It has a sandy beach, a pier, casual restaurants, shops, and that old-school summer feeling that makes you want to slow down.

According to recent reports, this is not a polished luxury escape, and that is exactly the point. Port Dover is relaxed, nostalgic, and easy. It’s the kind of place where a hot dog, a walk by the water, and a sunset can be the whole proposal.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Use Port Dover as the starting point for a Lake Erie mini road trip to Turkey Point, Port Rowan, or local wineries and breweries.

Best for: paddling, cottage-country scenery, lift locks, museums, Indigenous art, and relaxed exploringDrive from Toronto: about 1.5 to 2 hoursSuggested day: Visit the Peterborough Lift Lock, explore the Canadian Canoe Museum, paddle or walk along the water, then stop for food or local shopping before heading home.

Peterborough sits at the gateway to the Kawarthas and gives you a taste of cottage country without driving too far. It’s a good choice if you want water, history, culture, and a relaxed pace.

In a recent development, the Peterborough Lift Lock is the classic stop, and the Canadian Canoe Museum adds a meaningful look at paddling history and Indigenous craftsmanship. The area also has riverside trails, breweries, and access to the Trent-Severn Waterway.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Don’t treat Peterborough as just a place to pass through on the way to cottage country. It has enough to fill a full day.

Best for: skiing, hiking, biking, spa days, village atmosphere, and four-season adventureDrive from Toronto: about 2 to 2.5 hoursSuggested day: Spend the morning hiking, skiing, or visiting Scenic Caves, then explore Blue Mountain Village and finish with Scandinave Spa if you want a slower end to the day.

Blue Mountain and Collingwood are technically a longer day trip, but they are worth it if you start early. In winter, Blue Mountain is one of the most popular ski and snowboard areas near Toronto. In summer, it becomes a hub for hiking, biking, patios, and outdoor activities.

Scenic Caves, Blue Mountain Village, the waterfront in Collingwood, and Scandinave Spa all make this area easy to customize depending on your travel style.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: If you want the day to feel less rushed, pick one main activity. Don’t try to ski, spa, hike, shop, and eat your way through the whole region in one day.

Best for: beach days, families, swimming, paddleboarding, summer energy, and easy sand-and-sun escapesDrive from Toronto: about 2 hoursSuggested day: Arrive early, set up on the beach, swim or paddleboard, grab lunch nearby, and stay for sunset if traffic is manageable.

Wasaga Beach is one of Ontario’s classic summer day trips. It is known for its long sandy shoreline, shallow water, and big beach-day energy.

Sources indicate that this is a good choice when you want a simple day: cooler, towels, sunscreen, water, snacks, and sand. It can get very busy in summer, but that is part of the Wasaga experience.

Sources indicate that dave & Deb’s Tip: Go early on hot weekends. Parking and prime beach spots fill up fast. Book ahead with Ontario Parks or you can pay at parking lots.

Best for: lakes, paddling, fall colours, cottage-country scenery, breweries, and small townsDrive from Toronto: about 2 to 2.5 hoursSuggested day: Pick one town as your base, such as Gravenhurst, Bracebridge, or Huntsville, then add a lake stop, short hike, brewery, or boat cruise.

Muskoka is one of Ontario’s most famous cottage-country regions, with lakes, forests, docks, small towns, and that unmistakable smell of pine trees and campfires.

It is a bit of a long day trip from Toronto, but it works if you choose one area instead of trying to see the entire region. Gravenhurst, Bracebridge, Huntsville, and Port Carling all make good anchors.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Muskoka is better when you slow down. Choose one town, one lake, and one great food stop instead of racing between too many places.

Best for: wineries, beaches, food, art, romantic getaways, and summer road tripsDrive from Toronto: about 2.5 hoursSuggested day: Visit a winery or two, explore Picton or Wellington, stop at Sandbanks or a beach, and have dinner before heading back.

Prince Edward County is one of the best food-and-wine day trips from Toronto, though it also works beautifully as an overnight getaway. It has boutique wineries, cideries, beaches, farm stands, restaurants, art galleries, and small towns.

Industry observers note that sandbanks Provincial Park is the major beach draw, but the whole county is made for slow exploring. It’s ideal for couples, food lovers, and anyone who wants a countryside escape.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: For a true day trip, don’t overbook tastings. Pick one area of the county and enjoy it properly.

Best for: wilderness, paddling, hiking, fall colours, wildlife, and massive nature daysDrive from Toronto: about 3 hoursSuggested day: Leave before sunrise, choose one hiking trail or guided paddling experience, stop at a lookout or visitor centre, and head home before you are too tired.

Algonquin is a stretch as a day trip, but it can be done if you start early and keep the strategy simple. This is one of Ontario’s most iconic wilderness areas, with forests, lakes, hiking trails, canoe routes, and wildlife.

In a recent development, you won’t see all of Algonquin in a day, and you shouldn’t try. But a single hike, paddle, or scenic drive can still give you a taste of why the park is so special.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Algonquin is much better as an overnight, but if you only have one day, choose one trail or activity and make that the focus. Algonquin Outfitters offers excellent one-day guided tours .

In a recent development, no car? Book this Toronto to Algonquin Provincial Park private Tour.

Best for: The Grotto, Georgian Bay, hiking, turquoise water, cliffs, shipwrecks, and major adventure daysDrive from Toronto: about 3.5 to 4 hoursSuggested day: Leave very early, visit the Grotto or hike a section of the Bruce Trail, stop in Tobermory if time allows, and expect a long drive home.

In a recent development, bruce Peninsula National Park is one of the most spectacular places in Ontario, but it is a very long day trip from Toronto. The Grotto, Georgian Bay cliffs, turquoise water, and Bruce Trail scenery make it unforgettable.

According to recent reports, this is best for travellers who do not mind a long drive and a full day outdoors. For most people, it works better as an overnight getaway, but it can be done in a single ambitious day.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Reservations and parking rules matter here. Plan ahead, start early, and don’t wing it on a summer weekend.

Hamilton, Elora, and Niagara Falls are the best day trips from Toronto for waterfalls. Niagara Falls is the most famous, Hamilton has the greatest variety, and Elora gives you dramatic gorge scenery along the Grand River.

Industry observers note that wasaga Beach, Port Dover, Sandbanks in Prince Edward County, and the Toronto Islands are the best beach day trips from Toronto. Wasaga is best for a classic summer beach day, while Sandbanks is better if you want dunes and a longer road trip.

Industry observers note that niagara-on-the-Lake and Prince Edward County are the best wine-focused day trips from Toronto. Niagara-on-the-Lake is easier for a one-day trip, while Prince Edward County feels more relaxed if you can stay overnight.

According to recent reports, canada’s Wonderland, Toronto Islands, Niagara Falls, the Toronto Zoo, and Wasaga Beach are some of the best family-friendly day trips from Toronto. They offer easy activities, food options, and enough to fill a full day without complicated planning.

Sources indicate that milton, Hamilton, Elora, Algonquin Provincial Park, and Bruce Peninsula National Park are the best hiking day trips from Toronto. For an easy hike close to the city, choose Milton or Hamilton. For a bigger adventure, choose Algonquin or Bruce Peninsula.

According to recent reports, stratford, Elora, Paris, and Niagara-on-the-Lake are the best small-town day trips from Toronto. Each has a walkable centre, good food, independent shops, and enough charm to fill a relaxed day.

The best day trips from Toronto under 2 hours include Hamilton, Niagara Falls, Niagara-on-the-Lake, Elora, Stratford, Paris, Caledon, Milton, Kitchener-Waterloo, and Wasaga Beach. These are the easiest options if you want to leave in the morning and be back home by dinner.

Sources indicate that yes, Niagara Falls is one of the easiest and most popular day trips from Toronto. It takes about 90 minutes by car, and you can visit the falls, Journey Behind the Falls, Clifton Hill, the Niagara SkyWheel, and the Hornblower boat cruise in a single day if you start early.

Recent findings suggest that for nature close to the city, Hamilton’s waterfalls, Milton’s conservation areas, Elora Gorge, and Caledon are some of the best choices. For bigger wilderness, Algonquin Park and Bruce Peninsula are spectacular, but they work better as long day trips or overnight escapes.

Yes, but your options are more limited. Niagara Falls, Hamilton, Toronto Islands, and some towns along GO Transit or VIA Rail routes are possible without a car. For waterfalls, conservation areas, beaches, and rural towns, driving is usually much easier.

General 🌐 Cruiseindustrynews

Latest Update: 32 Hospitalized, None Missing After the American Heritage Capsizes

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read | Source: Cruiseindustrynews

💡 Key Takeaways
  • All passengers and crew have been accounted for after the American Cruise Lines’ American Heritage capsized in the Mississippi River at the Port of Newly introduced Orleans on Friday, officials said at a press conference that afternoon.
  • Sources indicate that thirty-two people were taken to local hospitals and none had critical injuries, according to officials.
  • Industry observers note that the tanker Atlantic Asphalt struck the American Heritage at about 12:30 p.m.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

All passengers and crew have been accounted for after the American Cruise Lines’ American Heritage capsized in the Mississippi River at the Port of Newly introduced Orleans on Friday, officials said at a press conference that afternoon.

Sources indicate that thirty-two people were taken to local hospitals and none had critical injuries, according to officials. This included 30 from the ship and two first responders, official noted.

Industry observers note that the tanker Atlantic Asphalt struck the American Heritage at about 12:30 p.m. The riverboat was docked at the port and passengers were disembarking.

“At this moment, the information that we have, we have zero people unaccounted for, which truly is a miracle on the Mississippi,” Fresh Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno said at the press conference.

Moreno stated the tanker lost control before it hit the cruise ship. Passengers began leaving the American Heritage after the collision.

“But while that was happening, the cruise ship began to sink, and then eventually the cruise ship toppled over and flipped,” she said. “Now, when that occurred, we started to have people in the water.”.

Moreno credited Port NOLA Harbor Police with going into the water to pull people out. She mentioned New Orleans firefighters put ladders over the dock to get people up, and other vessels on the river stopped to help.

Sources indicate that captain Melanie Burnham, commander of U.S. Coast Guard Sector Upcoming Orleans and captain of the port, remarked the Coast Guard sent small boats, cutters and helicopters to the search and rescue. She called the coordination between agencies “absolutely exceptional.”.

“Our focus here for the Coast Guard will now shift to reopening the river, because I did shut that down immediately as soon as we heard about the incident,” Burnham noted.

Recent findings suggest that louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry flew in from Baton Rouge by helicopter.

He stated President Trump had called him and told him, “Jeff, whatever Louisiana needs, we will make sure that they get.”.

Sources indicate that “It is a literal miracle on the Mississippi,” Landry said. “When you think about the population that was on that cruise ship and the ability for us to get them off, get them out of the water. Just in case you know, the Mississippi River is not some quiet pond.”.

Landry mentioned he and Moreno had met with passengers.

In a recent development, “We are going to make sure that they have a place to stay,” he mentioned. “We’re going to make sure that we get them to their loved ones in a very orderly fashion.”.

The governor noted the collision as an active investigation.

“We are going to get down to the bottom of exactly what happened here and make sure that we make any adjustments necessary so that the people that travel on the waterways here can know that they can do so in safety,” he said.

#107. Korean Air Adds Newark Flights From Incheon, Joining United & Air Premia

General 🌐 Onemileatatime

Korean Air Adds Newark Flights From Incheon, Joining United & Air Premia

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read | Source: Onemileatatime

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that korean Air has just quietly added a latest long haul route, as the airline will be adding service to Newark, New Jersey.
  • It has been revealed that as of May 22, 2027, Korean Air plans to launch daily nonstop flights between Seoul Incheon (ICN) and Newark.
  • KE97 Seoul Incheon to Newark departing 10:00PM arriving 11:00PMKE98 Newark to Seoul Incheon departing 1:00AM arriving 5:15AM (+1 day).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that korean Air has just quietly added a latest long haul route, as the airline will be adding service to Newark, New Jersey. What’s interesting is just how competitive this market has become, but it’s logical in the context of what’s going on at the airline (thanks to S_LEE for flagging this).

It has been revealed that as of May 22, 2027, Korean Air plans to launch daily nonstop flights between Seoul Incheon (ICN) and Newark. The flight will operate with the following schedule:.

KE97 Seoul Incheon to Newark departing 10:00PM arriving 11:00PMKE98 Newark to Seoul Incheon departing 1:00AM arriving 5:15AM (+1 day).

The 6,896-mile flight is blocked at 14hr to the United States, and 15hr15min to South Korea. Korean Air will use a Boeing 777-300ER for the route, featuring 277 seats, including eight first class seats, 42 business class seats, and 227 economy seats.

Recent findings suggest that this technically marks a service resumption, as Korean Air last served Newark through September 2001, but then suspended flights after the 9/11 terror attacks, and never resumed the flights. This upcoming service will complement Korean Air’s existing service to New York Kennedy (JFK), which typically operates twice daily.

On top of that, Korean Air’s destinations in the United States include Atlanta (ATL), Boston (BOS), Chicago (ORD), Dallas (DFW), Honolulu (HNL), Las Vegas (LAS), Los Angeles (LAX), San Francisco (SFO), Seattle (SEA), and Washington Dulles (IAD).

Recent findings suggest that interestingly, Korean Air faces quite a bit of competition in the market between Incheon and Newark. Going back several years, it’s a route that no airline served.

Industry observers note that however, that has changed in recent times. In May 2023, South Korean budget carrier Air Premia launched service in the market using a Boeing 787. Then in September 2026, United Airlines launched flights in the market, also using a Boeing 787. Korean Air’s timing is very similar to Air Premia’s in both directions, which isn’t too surprising.

Some people might be surprised to see Korean Air adding flights to Newark in addition to existing service to Kennedy (with no plans to reduce that service), but this actually seems pretty straightforward to me.

It has been revealed that keep in mind that Korean Air and Asiana have merged, and in the coming weeks, the two airlines will even take on the same brand. Historically these carriers were huge competitors, so of course in some markets they’ll be reducing capacity. In other words, the combined Korean Air won’t have quite as many frequencies to places like Los Angeles, Fresh York, and San Francisco, as the two airlines did separately.

That of course opens up the opportunity to serve more newly introduced markets, and clearly Newark was identified as one of those opportunities. Also keep in mind that Korean Air operates as part of a transpacific joint venture with Delta, so the airlines can coordinate fares and schedules, and it’s all about the combined depth and breadth of service.

If you’re looking at this from a Manhattan centric perspective, you might be surprised that the airline is bothering to serve both airports. However, service to Newark goes way beyond that, and the idea is that this flight is useful for serving parts of New Jersey, Pennsylvania, etc. Admittedly those flyers likely aren’t loyal to SkyTeam, but from a Korea point of sale perspective (especially with the number of people studying in the region), it makes sense.

As of May 2027, Korean Air will be launching daily flights from Seoul Incheon to Newark, complementing existing service to Kennedy. This means we’ll see three daily flights between Incheon and Newark on three different airlines… that’s quite the step up from the zero daily flights we saw several years back!

With Korean Air’s takeover of Asiana complete, it’s logical that the South Korean mega carrier would be looking at adding some latest markets, given the increased connectivity and scale of the operation.

According to recent reports, alaska Airlines' largest hub, Seattle (SEA), is about to gain four newly introduced nonstop domestic flights, as the airline adds services to Charlotte, Des Moines, Jacksonville and Norfolk. These routes will all operate daily.

According to aviation blogger Enilria, the oneworld carrier will expand its domestic reach from Washington State, following the airline's announcement of plans to operate flights to Guadalajara in Mexico and nonstop services from Anchorage to Tokyo.

#105. Avelo Brings First Commercial Flights to McKinney

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3 min read (654 words)

Avelo Brings First Commercial Flights to McKinney

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read | Source: Airlinegeeks

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Avelo operated its inaugural flight from McKinney National Airport in McKinney, Texas, on Wednesday.
  • Avelo Flight 1848, operated with a Boeing 737-800, was the first commercial airliner service from the airport to Fort Myers, Florida.
  • “We target the secondary airports of very large metropolitan areas where we can offer a different experience to the customers,” Avelo founder and CEO Andrew Levy mentioned in an interview with AirlineGeeks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Avelo operated its inaugural flight from McKinney National Airport in McKinney, Texas, on Wednesday.

Avelo Flight 1848, operated with a Boeing 737-800, was the first commercial airliner service from the airport to Fort Myers, Florida.

“We target the secondary airports of very large metropolitan areas where we can offer a different experience to the customers,” Avelo founder and CEO Andrew Levy mentioned in an interview with AirlineGeeks.

McKinney is the third airport in the Dallas/Fort Worth Metroplex to offer commercial service, with Dallas Love Field and Dallas/Forth Worth International Airport being the other two.

“For a lot of folks we’re going to be closer and a more convenient drive. And hopefully they’ll take advantage of that,” said McKinney airport director Ken Carley.

Carley said the airline has been wanting to be in the market since 2018. McKinney is the first new airport in Texas in 20 years to be certified for commercial air service.

According to recent reports, “We had to build all this infrastructure because it did not exist. There was nothing on this side of the airport. So it’s not just this building, it’s the ramp and the taxi lane and all of that stuff, the taxiway that connects to the runway system. So it was a building, all the infrastructure, and meeting all those requirements,” Carley said.

McKinney is about 30 miles northeast of Dallas in Collin County. Levy said the area is growing like crazy.

“What we’re going to offer people who live close to this airport is a very different experience than getting on the highways and driving all the way to DFW or going down to Love Field,” he said.

The Texas-based airline will serve 11 destinations from McKinney: Las Vegas, Tampa, Orlando, Fort Myers, Sarasota/Bradenton, Nashville, West Palm Beach, Fresh Orleans, Denver, Atlanta, and Fort Lauderdale.

“I think it’s phenomenal that Avelo has unveiled additional routes before they’ve even started service. That’s a testament, I think, to what they’re seeing in the response they’re getting from for bookings. So they think it’s a strong market,” Carley said.

Levy said the approach was to offer a lot of selections and get a better sense of the market.

“All the markets we’re serving have massive proven demand from this area. And so of course, the trick for us is just to get people to know we’re here and then give us a try,” Levy said.

McKinney is a crew base for Avelo, its fifth, with pilots, flight attendants, airport operations personnel, and aircraft technicians, about 150 people behind the operation, Levy said.

“The demand will dictate how we grow, if we grow, and how fast we grow. This is going to be based on, do customers like the service? Does it resonate with them? Are we serving a need that exists every other place we’ve been? We don’t have any trouble filling up airplanes. I think this market is just going to do great, but time will tell, and the consumer will let us know,” Levy said.

“Our focus is on building a business that’s sustainable for the long term,” he added. “And that means everything we do has to work. It’s got to work well.”.

According to recent reports, avelo currently offers service from DFW to Upcoming Haven, Connecticut. Levy said that service will continue but could move to McKinney at some point.

#104. The Great Sea Reef Is Fiji’s Wildest Dive, and a Fresh Frontier for Conservation

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9 min read (1744 words)
General 🌐 Cntraveler

The Great Sea Reef Is Fiji’s Wildest Dive, and a Fresh Frontier for Conservation

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read | Source: Cntraveler

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The bull shark appeared out of the blue in an instant.
  • Industry observers note that floating 60 feet below the surface in the South Pacific Ocean, I gave a shout of excitement through my scuba regulator when I saw it.
  • Author Samantha Falewée jumping in to dive the Great Sea Reef in Fiji.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The bull shark appeared out of the blue in an instant. And it was … fat.

Industry observers note that floating 60 feet below the surface in the South Pacific Ocean, I gave a shout of excitement through my scuba regulator when I saw it. Flanked by two remora fish, like bodyguards, the nine-foot bull shark turned in the water with surprising speed given its bulk, swimming just above the sandy sea floor. Deep water beckoned to its left. To the right, a wall of coral stretched upward above me in a mosaic of neon green, milky orange, and soft pink. A fellow diver floated nearby, clad in a speckled cerulean camouflage wetsuit, with wild hair floating around his mask. He flattened the side of his hand and placed it to the top of his head, the universal symbol for one of the biggest-ticket sightings a diver can hope for: shark. We’d be logging the bull into our census for sure.

Author Samantha Falewée jumping in to dive the Great Sea Reef in Fiji.

In a recent development, I was scuba diving in the Great Sea Reef (traditionally named Cakaulevu in Fijian), a 280-mile-long underwater paradise in northeast Fiji. Relatively unknown, with only a single scuba diving lodge that has direct access to it, this place is the third-largest coral reef system in the world. More than three-quarters of all coral species known to science live and grow here, as do more than half of all recognized fish.

Recent findings suggest that the Great Sea Reef, nicknamed the GSR, is also a growing hub of conservation research. In July 2026, a upcoming partnership between the Professional Association of Diving Instructors (PADI), PADI AWARE (the affiliated NGO), and the World Wildlife Fund (WWF) was launched to push community-backed ocean conservation. A key part of this is PADI AWARE’s new Global Shark & Ray Census, an ambitious project to collect data that PADI and WWF can use to inform governments, in Fiji and beyond, for the creation of new Marine Protected Areas. This recent collaboration made our morning shark sighting even more exciting—and meaningful.

“We are bringing together PADI’s 30-million-plus certified divers and 6,600 dive centers with WWF’s conservation work in over 100 countries,” states Ian Campbell, a driving force behind the collaboration and the programs director of PADI AWARE.

Recent findings suggest that in visiting the GSR, I was experiencing firsthand how travelers can experience this ecosystem and be a part of an innovative approach to protecting coral reefs. When I saw the lone bull shark, I wrote “bull shark: 1” in my waterproof notebook. The scribble was below my other excited notes from that same dive that read: “leopard shark! Amazing: 1” and “white-tipped reef shark: 2”. This underwater note-taking is the first step of the shark and ray census; the logging would happen when we returned to land.

Nukubati Resort, the sole property located on the Great Sea Reef.

Awaiting us, past a sandy beach and the angled heights of coconut trees, was Nukubati resort (pronounced Noo-koom-bah-ti). As the sole property located on the Great Sea Reef, Nukubati is the labor of love of two Fijian generations: It was opened in 1992 by Fiji-born Jenny Leewai and her Australian husband, Peter Bourke; and is now helmed by their daughter, Lara, with her husband, Leone, who was born and raised on the nearby Mali Island. Set against the slow pulse of the waves, styled in classic, custom-ordered cane palm furniture atop gleaming wooden floors, this little haven delivered a peaceful welcome after every dive.

Following a hot shower in my private bure, or bungalow, I rejoined the others at the broad open-air lounge, nicknamed the pavilion, which serves as the heart of this intimate resort. Jenny was already there, barefoot in a caftan with Champagne-colored pearls at her ears and fingers. Lara was there too, a red hibiscus flower tucked behind her ear. Lara and Leone’s young son, Masei, pattered past on the shining wooden floor, followed by a russet, tail-wagging dog, Bēbē.

Fijian tatavu, aka a traditional Fijian barbecue, served at Nukubati Resort.

In this deeply relaxed atmosphere, alfresco lunches can last hours. But as soon as we finished the meal—spicy pawpaw soup, followed by skewers of whitefish, pineapple, onions, and peppers in a bed of peanut sauce—I gathered with the other divers around a coffee table, where a weatherbeaten copy of Tropical Pacific Fish lay.

There, PADI regional manager Robyn Vincent and Leone led us through a lecture on sharks and rays, which ranged in topics from biology (many sharks are late bloomers: the remarkable greenland shark, for example, doesn’t reach sexual maturity until it’s 100 years old) to shark tourism (each year, roughly 500,000 people dive specifically to see sharks around the world, creating an industry valued at $314 million USD).

It has been revealed that then, we logged the sharks we’d just seen on the PADI AWARE app. Tapping through the details took just me six minutes as I marked our location (a dive site called “Fish Market”), our activity (options include diving, snorkeling, boating, fishing, and others), our maximum underwater depth (60 feet), and the number and species of sharks I’d seen (one bull shark, two gray reef sharks, one whitetip reef shark, and one zebra shark).

Since the census debuted in April 2026, more than 212,000 people have participated, submitting thousands of sightings from around the world. That data is vetted by employees at PADI AWARE, with scientific support from the James Cook University Centre for Sustainable Tropical Fisheries and Aquaculture in Australia. And what’s been logged so far is already being used: According to the university, some data has been implemented in a scientific paper at the moment under review, and verified images submitted to the app have helped confirm the presence of four shark and ray species in the neighboring country of Vanuatu. One of those four, the great hammerhead shark, is listed as ‘Critically Endangered’ on the IUCN Red List. These awe-inspiring animals can grow up to 20 feet long and engage in mysterious mating rituals, swimming in synchronous, ascending spirals. Their very existence off the reef-fringed, tropical shores of Vanuatu had been debated by scientists—until now.

During the author's five-day stay, she saw multiple species of sharks and rays on every single dive.

Thanks to PADI’s presence in remote natural places like these, the census’s fast-accumulating data could also have ramifications in PADI and WWF’s efforts to help reach the UN Convention on Biological Diversity’s 30x30, the goal to protect 30% of the world’s oceans by 2030.

Sources indicate that “WWF brings the political clout,” indicates Cheryl Bowlin, the founder of Reef Stewardship Frameworks, a community-based conservation nonprofit in Fiji. “They help encourage policy to create Marine Protected Areas.” Those Marine Protected Areas keep reefs healthy and safe for locals and travelers alike, and can provide latest forms of income to communities. (An academic paper published in 2025 found that turning unprotected dive sites into fully protected marine areas could generate more than $2 billion globally in direct tourism revenue—an income stream that largely incorporates dive centers owned and run by locals.).

Places like Nukubati Resort are a prime example of the reach and impact that travelers can have, even if they might not realize it at first. During my five-day stay there, I saw multiple species of sharks and rays—utterly wild, without human influence of feeding or baiting—on every single dive. Stats like that make scuba diehards and casual passersby alike take notice, especially since diving on the GSR is an option for all skill levels, from snorkelers to beginner divers (like me) to advanced. Visitors can experience top-notch diving and contribute helpful data at the same time.

In a recent development, “I’ve been working as a PADI scuba diving instructor since 2013, and I’ve traveled and dived extensively all over the world,” Vincent remarked as we motored out to a dive site the following day, where a gentle current carried us over seawalls coated with hard corals and neon fish. “The fact that we’ve seen sharks on every single dive, and we are the only boat here, is incredible. There could be 50 dive centers here, 50 other dive boats.”.

The reef holds significance in local heritage, too. “The name of the Great Sea Reef in our northern dialect is Bainivualiku, which means the fence of the north,” said Leone. We sat at Nukubati, along with Leone’s wife and business partner, Lara, not far from the beach one afternoon, after another morning of glorious diving. “In the old days, the reef protected our community from sailing invaders who wanted to come in,” he said. The Great Sea Reef has been celebrated in songs and stories amongst regional communities for generations. Today, Leone and other locals are recognized as traditional stakeholders in the GSR’s future. To them, “The reef is our heart and soul,” Leone said.

In a recent development, that unshakable faith is evident in the family’s nurturing of Nukubati, which has withstood cyclones, a fire, the COVID-19 pandemic, and more. Throughout the trials the property has come out the other side, a timeless hideaway that accommodates a maximum of just 14 guests. The strong family and community bonds have kept it going; 100 percent of the Nukubati staff are local. Sustainability is another defining aspect, as Nukubati has run on solar panels, a system hand-engineered by co-founder Peter, since its opening day in the 1990s. Fast forward to now: In September 2026, Nukubati and its in-house operator, Great Sea Reef Divers, were recognized as a PADI Eco Center, a designation awarded to properties that demonstrate a significant commitment and investment to conservation and sustainability.

Now, after their dives, Leone and his team log the sharks and rays they’ve seen in the upcoming global census, and encourage visitors to join. “There's no looking back now,” Leone noted, rubbing his hands together. Ahead of him, the Great Sea Reef—colossal, colorful, teeming with sea life and yet empty of humans—waited just below the surface.

Airports and transit stations are full of QR codes: Wi-Fi, directions, tickets, luggage storage, forms, lounge access, and service information. Travel scams often happen when travelers are in a hurry. If you need wifi, a taxi, some food, QR codes are often the easiest way to catch you off guard.

Before your phone opens anything, look at the QR code itself.

Industry observers note that first, do not panic. Scanning a QR code does not automatically mean your information has been stolen. The bigger risk usually begins when you enter payment information, type a password, download a file, or provide personal details.

Close the page immediately if the link looks wrong, the message creates urgency, or the site asks for information you did not expect to provide.

Do not download an unfamiliar app or file from a QR code.

If you entered credit card information, contact your bank or card issuer using the official number on the back of your card or through the official banking app.

According to recent reports, if you entered a password, change it through the official website or app. If you reused that password anywhere else, change it there too.

According to recent reports, watch for follow-up messages. A scammer who has some of your information may later pretend to be your bank, hotel, airline, rental car organization, or payment provider.

Report the fake QR code to the business, parking authority, hotel, airport, or local authority so they can remove it.

No. QR codes are part of modern travel, and many are perfectly safe.

QR codes are convenient, but convenience is exactly what scammers are using against travellers.

#102. JetBlue’s New First Class Is Missing A Cabin Divider… But Why?!?

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7 min read (1448 words)
General 🌐 Onemileatatime

JetBlue’s New First Class Is Missing A Cabin Divider… But Why?!?

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read | Source: Onemileatatime

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that in the coming weeks, JetBlue will be introducing a domestic first class product for the first time, which will be known as BlueFirst.
  • Sources indicate that the first aircraft has now been retrofitted with the new cabins, and it appears that JetBlue had a media day today for this showing off both the new hard and soft product.
  • I don’t want to bury the lede here, so let me get right to it — on planes with BlueFirst, JetBlue won’t have any sort of a cabin divider between first class and the rest of the cabin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in the coming weeks, JetBlue will be introducing a domestic first class product for the first time, which will be known as BlueFirst. This is an exciting and long overdue development, and I trust it will help JetBlue’s revenue performance, especially given how efficiently planes are being reconfigured (by reducing legroom in economy).

Sources indicate that the first aircraft has now been retrofitted with the new cabins, and it appears that JetBlue had a media day today for this showing off both the new hard and soft product. We already largely knew what to expect, but what stands out to me is the one thing that’s missing, which I really can’t make sense of.

I don’t want to bury the lede here, so let me get right to it — on planes with BlueFirst, JetBlue won’t have any sort of a cabin divider between first class and the rest of the cabin. It’s not just that there isn’t a curtain, but there’s not even a divider hanging from the overhead bins.

JetBlue unveiled its fresh domestic first-class seats Wednesday as more of the country’s carriers bet on the premium travel boom to make them profitable again.Read more: https://t.co/5o3k2Ru5R9 pic.twitter.com/1BTcLVOr7s.

I guess this also explains the very creative angles of the renderings that have been released up until now, which clearly try to avoid highlighting this reality.

I really can’t make sense of this decision. I know we no longer live in an era where there are real, full bulkheads between cabins, since that’s not efficient. But just installing a small, flimsy divider, along with a curtain, costs very little, doesn’t weigh a lot, etc.

Recent findings suggest that to be clear, this isn’t about “oh, I don’t want to be seen by anyone.” Instead, it’s about managing traffic to and from the forward lavatory. At US airlines, the most common policy is that on domestic flights, you can use any lavatory onboard the aircraft, even in a different cabin. There are some exceptions, including for JetBlue Mint, but that’s also easier to enforce thanks to how the A321 is configured, with a lavatory behind Mint, in front of economy.

Industry observers note that I’m not sure if JetBlue intends to reserve the forward lavatory for BlueFirst passengers, but either way, you can expect there will be a steady stream of passengers lining up to use the forward lavatory. So it’s not even about potentially not having a dedicated lavatory, but instead it’s about just constantly having people standing in the aisle right by your seat. This will also make the life of the first class flight attendant more difficult.

In a recent development, take Aer Lingus AerSpace, for example, which is Aer Lingus’ premium product on short haul flights in Europe. It’s simply the first row of seats with blocked middles, and no divider between that and the rest of the plane. The problem is that if you’re seated in the aisle in AerSpace, you basically just have someone’s butt in your face the entire flight. You’re almost better off not booking the product, just to avoid that.

Anyway, I can’t really make sense of this decision, so I’d be fascinated to know what the logic was. There’s not another US airline with first class that has no separation between first class and economy. Spirit’s “Big Front Seat” didn’t have any divider, but that also wasn’t first class — it was just an, ummm, big front seat.

Similarly, Breeze Airways’ “Nicest” product also doesn’t have a divider, but it’s also not a separate cabin.

It has been revealed that CNBC’s Phil Le Beau was onboard JetBlue’s first BlueFirst A320 with CEO Joanna Geraghty. I like Le Beau, but this interview is also the perfect example of why I just don’t really value interviewing airline executives in a traditional sense.

Sources indicate that le Beau asked Geraghty a good question — “did you wait too long to add a first class?” If we are being honest, there’s only one correct answer, which is OF COURSE. Like, unarguably, JetBlue was at least years late, if not a decade late, to introducing first class. That’s not even Geraghty’s fault, it’s that previous CEO Robin Hayes was perhaps one of the least focused CEOs the US airline industry has ever seen.

Geraghty’s answer, though, was “I don’t think we’ve waited too long, we’ve had Mint for a very long time, it just takes time with some of these products to roll them out.” I get it — nobody wants to be, like “we screwed up and waited too long, but I mainly blame the guy before me.”.

Seriously, though, if she really doesn’t think JetBlue waited too long to commit to introducing first class, then I’d question how observant the executive team has been of the industry. I mean, Frontier confirmed it would introduce first class before JetBlue, which should tell you all you need to know. Oh, and Frontier will even have divider, even if it doesn’t have recline, food, or drinks!

Also, the below screen grab from the interview gave me a chuckle….

It has been revealed that jetBlue’s BlueFirst class is entering service soon, which is exciting. I’m a huge fan of JetBlue, and I think historically they’ve done a great job with both their hard and soft product, and have great attention to detail. So I’m just a bit puzzled as to how they came to the conclusion that there was no need to introduce a cabin divider between first class and economy.

It’s not about “privacy,” or anything like that, but instead it’s about trying to minimize foot traffic, and people congregating in the aisle waiting for the lavatory. You don’t want to pay extra to sit in first class, only to have people standing in the aisle the entire flight waiting to use the bathroom.

JetBlue will be the first airline in the US with first class to not have any sort of a cabin divider, and I can’t make sense of that.

#101. How I Got My Visa to France

📅 16 Feb 2026 • ⏱️ 11 min read (2222 words)
General 🌐 Nomadicmatt

How I Got My Visa to France

📅 16 Feb 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read | Source: Nomadicmatt

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that I’ve been in love with France ever since my first trip to Bordeaux in 2010.
  • But that love became an obsession when, after Bordeaux, I stepped out of the Paris metro and onto the Champs-Élysées.
  • In a recent development, since then, Paris has had a firm grip on my heart.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that I’ve been in love with France ever since my first trip to Bordeaux in 2010. Friends I had met back in Thailand demonstrated me around the area and introduced me to French culture. It was my first time in France and I loved the food, the wine, and the people.

But that love became an obsession when, after Bordeaux, I stepped out of the Paris metro and onto the Champs-Élysées. The lights, the energy, the mystique! There was magic in the air. I felt like I had known the city my entire life and I was simply returning home.

In a recent development, since then, Paris has had a firm grip on my heart. Over the years, I spent countless visits exploring France and Paris in particular. I’ve run tours in the city and I spent a few months living there in 2019.

Last August, after yet another sojourn, I thought to myself, “What if I moved back?”.

Industry observers note that I was growing a bit tired of the NYC dating scene, the rising cost of living, and felt like, creatively, I was in a rut. With AI coming for creators like me and the industry changing, I was a little lost on what, career-wise, would come next.

And Paris seemed like the best place to go.

It’s cheaper than NYC, I had friends there already, I’ve always wanted to learn French, it would make a great base for exploring Europe, and I could start writing my next book there. There’s nothing like a change in scenery to get the creativity flowing!

But the question remained: how do you move to France?

After all, they don’t have a digital nomad visa, and you’re limited to three months if you visit on your regular Schengen tourist visa.

Well, it turns out that it’s not actually that hard. (And while I can only speak for Americans, I suspect the criteria are similar for Canadians, Aussies, Kiwis, and other “developed” nations.).

If you want to move to France, you have four main options:.

It has been revealed that the student visa is pretty straightforward. You need to enroll in a full-time university program and show you have enough funds to support yourself (around 600 Euros per month). A friend is at the moment there on this visa, as she is doing a nine-month intensive French program to become fluent. You still have to apply for the visa, but if you’re enrolled in an accredited school, you’ll likely get approved. Another benefit to this visa is that you can work part-time on it!

Industry observers note that but this visa is contingent on being in school, so if you leave or quit, it’s voided. However, when you are done, you can change this to a “job seeker” visa, which can give you up to another six months in France (or more depending on how long your program was).

According to recent reports, I thought about applying for the entrepreneur visa, but the application process is pretty complex and can take months to be approved. You have to set up your business in France — and that is a lot of paperwork. You have to show that your business makes money, has clients (at least one of them being French), and can support you full-time (you have to make at least the French minimum wage). They will scrutinize your assets and financials a lot and you’ll need to register your business in France and pay French taxes.

Additionally, France offers a talent visa. If you’re an expert in your field (with verifiable accreditations and accolades), this could be a good visa to apply for, especially if you initiative to stay in France for a long time and want to physically work there. But, again, you’ll need to have some source of income and plan to do physical business in France. If you’re not an academic but someone in the arts, you have to show how you are going to add to the “culture of France” in some way.

While I would meet the requirements for both those visas, the process for either would have been time-consuming, and, since I’m not sure France is going to be my forever home, I decided not to go through that process.

So I went with the long-term visitor visa, officially called VLS-TS visiteur. This allows me to stay up to 12 months in France and is renewable in the country. It does come with a lot of restrictions, however: I can’t physically work here and I am not allowed into the French social welfare system.

It’s also the visa a lot of Americans (and most retirees) are coming in on. If you have passive income or retirement savings and just want to live in France, this is a good option for you. It allows you to set up a bank account and it can be renewed pretty much indefinitely.

Recent findings suggest that the paperwork for this visa (which I’ll get into in a bit) essentially comes down to whether or not you can support yourself. French authorities want to make sure you won’t be a burden on the system.

My biggest question centered around whether or not I could “work” on this visa. A lot of creators and digital nomads are applying for — and getting — this visa.

But remember: you aren’t allowed to work on this visa so how are you going to work if you can’t work?

So let me take a moment to talk about “work” from a legal standpoint.

It has been revealed that as I mentioned, there’s no digital nomad visa that allows you to work in France. And the French tax office remarked last July that remote work is considered taxable — but there are no official laws that say so. That’s just their opinion and there’s been no progress in codifying that opinion. In fact, my visa doesn’t even come with a tax number, so I can’t be taxed. I couldn’t pay taxes even if I wanted to.

The visa office asks how you’ll support yourself when you are in France and one of the sources of income they accept is “income from work.” I was very open that my means of support would be the income from this blog and my books.

The system there really hasn’t caught up to remote work. It still defines “work” as something you do physically that could take away a job from a French person.

In a recent development, so could I run walking tours in Paris? Nope. Could you work at a café? Nope.

According to recent reports, but does writing this blog post count as work? After all, no one is paying for it. It’s a free resource. Does going to a café to work on the next great American novel count? What about my weekly newsletter that has affiliate links (that generate income) in it? Is writing that considered work?

It has been revealed that the gray area is considerable, so the best thing to do is to talk to a lawyer. I recommend Daniel Tostado (yes, that’s his real name), one of the biggest American-French immigration lawyers in Paris. He has a huge law firm and regularly meets with government officials to clarify the rules on this. He gave me some solid advice.

For this long-term visitor visa, the application process is pretty easy. You go to the French government website, fill out your application, take the application number to the TLScontact website, and make an appointment. (France outsources the appointment process to this company, which then sends everything to the French consulate for approval.).

The main things you’ll want to demonstrate are that you have accommodation for 90 days on your application and enough income to support yourself. They just want to make sure you aren’t going to be a burden on the system. I went overboard. Here’s what I brought to my appointment:.

Sources indicate that I didn’t need the second bank account, tax returns, or W-2 (they weren’t required) but the woman at the appointment said the more proof you had the better and it wouldn’t hurt. And another friend who got this visa didn’t bring anything beyond what was asked in the application form. But I wanted to take no chances!

In a recent development, at the appointment, the staff double-checks your paperwork, takes your biometric data, collects the fees, and then sends your passport to the embassy for processing. Officially, it takes up to 15 days to process your visa, but everyone I know seems to get it back within a week.

The worst part was not knowing if you are approved until your passport is returned. While you can track the progress of your application, you don’t know the verdict until your passport is back in your hands. While I was waiting (and anxiously spiraling), I looked on Reddit and found that most denials were for lack of income or issues with their accommodation, which seem to be the two most notable things to have perfect on your application.

Once you get your visa back, you can enter France any time after the start date. After you enter, you have 90 days to register your visa with the state (they give you a little QR code with instructions). This allows you to “officially” be on this long-term visa. (It’s a more paperwork kind of thing.).

Once that is done, there’s nothing else to do and you can stay in France (and Europe) until your visa expires!

It has been revealed that so, if you’re considering moving to France, these are your options. But, as always, I’m not a lawyer and this is not legal advice. In regard to work and other complications or questions, it’s crucial that you seek legal counsel and get their expert opinion!

The  is one of the most recognizable premium travel rewards cards on the market, offering everything from airport lounge access and hotel elite status to a long list of travel and lifestyle statement credits.

But with an $895 annual fee (see rates and fees), it's also a significant investment.

Recent findings suggest that the Amex Platinum offers plenty of opportunities to offset that cost, especially if you travel frequently and can take advantage of its statement credits. However, many of its benefits come with restrictions, and getting the full value requires some effort.

Recent findings suggest that so, who can actually get enough value from the Amex Platinum to justify its annual fee? Let's take a closer look at who should — and shouldn't — consider adding this card to their wallet.

For frequent travelers, airport lounge access is one of the biggest reasons to consider the .

The card offers access to one of the most extensive airport lounge networks available through a credit card, making it especially valuable if you spend a lot of time in airports.

Cardmembers can access American Express Centurion Lounges, receive a Priority Pass Select membership (enrollment required) and visit Delta Sky Clubs when flying on eligible same-day Delta flights. Delta Sky Club access is limited to 10 visits per year unless you spend $75,000 on eligible purchases in a calendar year to unlock unlimited visits. Access is subject to eligibility requirements.

Amex also operates Centurion Lounges at more than 20 airports, so the benefit can be particularly valuable if you live near or frequently connect through an airport with one.

Industry observers note that if you travel frequently and would otherwise pay for lounge access, the Platinum could help you save money while making your time at the airport more comfortable. And when combined with the card's other travel benefits and statement credits, lounge access can help make the $895 annual fee easier to justify.

While the is best known for its premium travel benefits, it also offers a growing list of lifestyle statement credits that can help offset its $895 annual fee.

According to recent reports, for example, cardmembers can receive up to $400 in Resy statement credits each calendar year (distributed as up to $100 per quarter) at eligible U.S. Resy restaurants* and up to $300 in Lululemon statement credits* (up to $75 quarterly) at U.S. stores (excluding outlets) and online.

The card also offers up to $300 annually in digital entertainment statement credits* (up to $25 monthly) for eligible subscriptions, along with up to $120 annually toward an Uber One membership to fully cover an auto-renewing $96 annual or $9.99 monthly membership*.

If you're already spending money on dining, shopping and entertainment in these categories, the credits can provide meaningful value without requiring you to change your spending habits.

Recent findings suggest that however, many of these benefits are divided into monthly or quarterly credits, so you'll need to keep track of when to use them. The Platinum is a particularly good fit for someone who doesn't mind managing these benefits and can consistently take advantage of them year-round.

Related: How to maximize benefits with the American Express Platinum.

The Amex Platinum can also be a valuable addition to your wallet if you regularly stay at Hilton, Marriott or luxury hotels.

According to recent reports, cardmembers receive complimentary Hilton Honors Gold and Marriott Bonvoy Gold Elite status, which can provide benefits such as bonus points on stays and potential room upgrades. You'll also receive Leaders Club Sterling status with The Leading Hotels of the World, a collection of independent luxury hotels. Enrollment is required for select benefits.

Beyond elite status, one of the Platinum's most valuable hotel-related perks is its up to $600 annual lodging statement credit (up to $300 semiannually).

Cardmembers can receive up to $300 in statement credits every six months on eligible prepaid bookings through American Express Travel®, including stays at Fine Hotels + Resorts and The Hotel Collection properties, as well as select Airbnb Luxe stays.

Sources indicate that the Hotel Collection and Airbnb Luxe require a minimum two-night stay, and beginning Jan. 1, 2027, Fine Hotels + Resorts bookings will also require at least two nights to qualify for the lodging credit.

Fine Hotels + Resorts bookings also come with valuable benefits, including daily breakfast for two, guaranteed 4 p.m. late checkout, room upgrades when available and a property credit valued at $100.

If you regularly book these types of stays, the lodging credit and additional perks can go a long way toward offsetting the card's annual fee. Just be sure to compare prices with booking directly, since rates through Amex Travel aren't always the lowest.

Related: How to maximize the Amex Platinum hotel statement credit.

Chase's unofficial 5/24 rule generally makes applicants ineligible for many Chase cards if they've opened five or more personal credit cards across issuers within the past 24 months.

Travelers who are still eligible for Chase cards may want to prioritize products such as the (see rates and fees) or (see rates and fees) before exceeding that threshold.

If you've already built a collection of Chase rewards cards, the Amex Platinum could be worth considering as your next premium travel card.

The card also earns Membership Rewards points, giving you access to a separate collection of airline and hotel transfer partners that can complement an existing Chase Ultimate Rewards strategy.

Sources indicate that many people just starting in the points world underestimate the stringency of Chase’s 5/24 rule. If you're just getting started with travel rewards and remain under Chase's 5/24 threshold, you may want to think carefully before applying for the Amex Platinum.

Industry observers note that opening the card could count toward your 5/24 total and potentially limit your eligibility for Chase cards in the future. That could mean missing out on valuable welcome offers or benefits from cards you planned to open later.

However, once you get over 5/24, it may be hard to get back under, and there’s a massive opportunity cost in doing so. Having a blueprint and sticking to it will serve you well in the long term.

In a recent development, of course, that doesn't mean everyone under 5/24 should avoid the Platinum. If its benefits are a particularly good fit for your travel habits, it may still make sense.

The provides 5 Membership Rewards points per dollar spent on flights booked directly with airlines or with American Express Travel (on up to $500,000 of spending each calendar year, then 1 point per dollar spent).

A card like the or (see rates and fees) may be a better fit because their broader travel earning categories can include eligible third-party airfare bookings.

The offers a long list of statement credits, but that doesn't necessarily mean every cardholder will get enough value from them to justify the $895 annual fee.

Following the card's 2025 refresh, several of its benefits are geared toward specific lifestyle purchases, including dining at Resy restaurants, shopping at Lululemon and purchasing an Oura Ring. (Cardmembers receive up to a $200 Oura Ring statement credit each calendar year. This statement credit applies to ring purchases only and doesn't cover subscriptions. Enrollment is required.).

Industry observers note that many of these credits also come with restrictions. For example, the Resy and Lululemon credits are distributed quarterly, meaning you'll need to use them throughout the year rather than all at once.

If you don't already spend money with these merchants, or you don't want to keep track of multiple credits and enrollment requirements, the Platinum may not be the best fit.

Before applying, carefully consider just how much these credits are worth to you; if they provide little to no value, another Amex card might be a better fit.

Related: 4 different flavors of Amex Platinum — which one is right for you?

Business owners with substantial expenses may find that is a better fit than the personal Platinum.

Although both cards carry an $895 annual fee (see rates and fees), their earning rates and statement credits differ in ways that could make one more valuable than the other.

For example, the Business Platinum earns 2 points per dollar spent on eligible purchases in select business categories and on purchases of $5,000 or more, on up to $2 million in combined eligible purchases per calendar year, then 1 point per dollar.

Sources indicate that the Business Platinum also provides up to $1,150 in statement credits per calendar year for U.S. Dell purchases: up to $150 each calendar year and an additional $1,000 statement credit after spending $5,000 on Dell purchases with the same card each calendar year (enrollment required).

Recent findings suggest that you can also access the Pay with Points redemption option on the Business Platinum card, which gets you a 35% bonus for eligible flights with your selected airline using your Amex points (up to 1 million points back per calendar year). This is notably not available on the personal Amex Platinum.

These business-focused benefits may be more useful for someone with significant company expenses, while the personal Platinum may be a better fit for travelers who can maximize its lifestyle credits.

Recent findings suggest that fresh cardmembers can find out their offer and may be eligible for as high as 175,000 bonus points after spending $12,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.).

Based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, that bonus could be worth up to $3,500, which is nearly four times the card's $895 annual fee.

While this is the card's standard welcome offer, now could still be a good time to apply if you're eligible for an offer you're happy with and can comfortably meet the spending requirement without making unnecessary purchases.

Just make sure you'll also get enough value from the card's ongoing benefits to justify its annual fee beyond the first year.

Related: The best time to apply for Amex cards based on offer history.

The offers an impressive lineup of premium travel benefits and statement credits, but its $895 annual fee means it won't make sense for everyone.

For frequent travelers who value airport lounge access and luxury hotel perks, and can consistently use the card's lifestyle credits, there's plenty of potential to get more value than the annual fee.

On the other hand, travelers who prefer straightforward rewards or don't regularly use the card's benefits may find better value with a lower-annual-fee option.

Ultimately, the Platinum is worth considering if its benefits fit your existing spending and travel habits — not because of the total advertised value of its credits.
