United Airlines Bans “AI Agents,” Claims It’s To “Protect Customers”

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read | Source: Onemileatatime

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that united Airlines has just banned travelers from using “AI Agents” to book or service tickets (thanks to TravelinWilly for flagging this).
  • United Airlines has today updated its contract of carriage, which are the terms that passengers have to agree to when they book a ticket.
  • The use of AI Agents to make, modify or service a Ticket, and/or to purchase any service or product.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that united Airlines has just banned travelers from using “AI Agents” to book or service tickets (thanks to TravelinWilly for flagging this). That’s an interesting stance for United, easily the country’s most tech savvy airline, to take. So what’s actually going on here?

United Airlines has today updated its contract of carriage, which are the terms that passengers have to agree to when they book a ticket. In the section about prohibited practices at the airline, the carrier added the following:.

The use of AI Agents to make, modify or service a Ticket, and/or to purchase any service or product.

The “AI Agents” term is defined by United as follows:.

In a recent development, AI Agent means any software or service, including but not limited to an AI assistant, AI agent or AI-enabled browser that takes autonomous or semi-autonomous action, whether or not Passenger or another individual supervises or approves its actions, to discover, search for, book, purchase, ticket, service or manage any product or service offered by or through United, including flights, seats, upgrades, ancillary products and partner products, on behalf of or at the instruction of Passenger or other individual. AI Agents include but are not limited to: (i) AI assistants built into social media, messaging, search or other consumer platforms; (ii) AI-enabled browsers and standalone AI agents; and (iii) any third-party AI assistant that accesses United through a tool, application or connection provided by a travel agency or other intermediary.

It has been revealed that united even put out a press release about this change, claiming that it’s making the change to “protect” customers. Here’s part of the explanation:.

Sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles. Plus, these automated AI actions have the potential to violate FAA and DOT regulations – as an example, flight check-in requires human acknowledgment that bags do not contain banned substances like explosives.

United claims it’s taking steps to restrict this kind of access, both directly within its digital platforms, and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators, to prohibit use by unauthorized, third party personal AI agents or assistants.

Recent findings suggest that it goes without saying that use of AI is becoming exponentially more popular in recent times, and is a force to be reckoned with. It’s anyone’s guess just how far it goes, in terms of how much the average person uses it in their everyday life.

In a recent development, there are certainly aspects of AI that are incredibly annoying, whether you look at it as an individual or a business. Admittedly I’m biased, but I’m so tired of feeling like half of what I’m reading online (whether on social media or websites) is written by a computer and not a human. It even extends to things like TripAdvisor reviews.

It’s also frustrating how many people write 30 paragraph emails nowadays, which are clearly 90% AI. I don’t really understand how that makes anyone’s life better. As far as I’m concerned, just give me the bullet points you fed your AI buddy, and we’ll all be better off for it. Anyway, rant over, back to United….

Recent findings suggest that I suspect United’s real motive here is that it doesn’t want AI automatically being able to track and reprice flights (and then glitch vouchers for passengers), or being able to too closely compare overall value on different airlines. For that matter, it probably just doesn’t want a third party getting that much data on the airline, not to mention that all of this can take a considerable toll on servers, if this scales.

But here’s what I find most interesting — the way this rule is written strikes me as being incredibly broad, no? Not to repeat the quote again, but this is the part I’m referencing, in particular:.

AI Agent means any software or service, including but not limited to an AI assistant, AI agent or AI-enabled browser that takes autonomous or semi-autonomous action, whether or not Passenger or another individual supervises or approves its actions, to discover, search for, book, purchase, ticket, service or manage any product or service offered by or through United, including flights, seats, upgrades, ancillary products and partner products, on behalf of or at the instruction of Passenger or other individual.

Any software that automatically “discovers” or searches for any product or service offered by United would include all award search tools (along with all kinds of other businesses), no? Is that actually the intent here, or does United just initiative to selectively enforce rules? We did see Air Canada engage in a battle over this a few years back, so is United planning something similar?

Industry observers note that united Airlines has today updated its rules to ban “AI Agents,” and the airline even put out a press release about it. The firm claims it’s making this change to protect customers and their accounts, as AI bots could have unintended consequences.

Many people are understandably skeptical of that explanation, as I imagine the airline also wants to ban these kinds of things to help people reprice tickets, get better fares, etc. For that matter, based on how broadly the definition is written, it seems that even things like award search engines would be banned.

In a recent development, membership is free and takes no more information than commenting as a guest. Earn status points for good contributions, and see fewer ads as your status grows.

Your feedback is important in helping us keep our community safe.

The comments on this page have not been provided, reviewed, approved or otherwise endorsed by any advertiser, and it is not an advertiser's responsibility to ensure posts and/or questions are answered.

Industry observers note that on one hand, it's easy to look at United's motive here. They don't want to lose revenue, and AI / MCP capabilities can easily get around some of the scraping restrictions that they've built over the last decade. But a level deeper, we're also seeing the same thing in finance. And retail. Heck, AI is even eating Google's core business. There's probably a good degree of fear from every industry that something massive is coming and rather than learn to adapt, take risks and aim to thrive, they do what America does best: ban it and tell you it's for security.

Recent findings suggest that the future is here. I had 1 of my AI agents (Insight) monitoring hotel reservations. It found cheaper rates on the same dates for 2 existing reservations & asked if I would like it to book the latest reservation & cancel the old. I agreed. A hotel in London is > $200 cheaper. One in Perth $10 cheaper (ha ha). But since there was little time cost to me to let it rebook the Perth reservation, I said go ahead. But I gave permission first & reviewed the new reservations & cancellations afterward.

In a recent development, personally, I am glad they imposed this ban. Whatever their reason is I don't care. As a iT security guy, allowing an agent to interface with booking opens up soooooo many security breach potentials and nearly impossible to explain it to a exec or govt official in a way they would understand. To the point the regulators would just dismiss what they don't understand as fear mongering. Companies just cannot randomly deloy AI features. To date none of them including big tech are treating ai security with any seriousness. The only security right now is good enough for optics and counting on the public not understanding how this stuff works. All the scamming attempts we get now will be magnify by 1000x and the speed of the scale will increase dramatically. Binance getting hacked and losing $6B should be a big big warning given that they have much more security than an airline. I am tell you unequivocally airline data security is laughable. United airline for example, their IT don't even know what 2 FA actually is. Their website have some lame security and they call it 2FA not even realizing what they implemented actually made their security worse. These ceos think AI is magic. They're going to get a very hard lesson on AI and AI security. The one blessing I have is that because I churn credit cards so often I'm not concern about cc data breaches or stolen card #. But everything else, we're in for some pain.

I think this is likely a combination of pricing data protection (there are sites today that have a lot of access but there are limits to how it can be leveraged individually, whereas you could have your own agent do data scrapes specific to flights you want to book), and getting ahead of the potential for thousands of individual agents scraping airline websites and either causing stability challenges or running up their hosting costs. They also want to protect their own ability to create their own agents that have unique access to their data (and potentially charging for that). Amazon has done the same thing - and went as far as to limit the descriptions and details they provide in order emails now so Google can't scrape the data from Gmail accounts.

Sources indicate that it's pretty clear that when an AI agent books a ticket for the user, United is not liable for mistake. What's more interesting, though, is if there's a third party service like cheapflights.ai or something that the user can pay to book them a good flight. If the website screws up, is the user or cheapflights.ai liable? More abstractly, in an agentic SaaS scenario, does the agent owner or the agent operator bear liability?

#98. Breaking: America’s Most Famous Ocean Liner Is Sent to a Watery Grave—and a New Life

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8 min read (1619 words)
General 🌐 Cntraveler

Breaking: America’s Most Famous Ocean Liner Is Sent to a Watery Grave—and a New Life

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read | Source: Cntraveler

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that in a secluded corner of Mobile, Alabama, past train tracks, deserted lots, and a county jail, sits a treasure of American history: the SS United States.
  • At nearly 1,000 feet long, the SS United States has always occupied a world of superlatives.
  • Passengers on the maiden voyage included Margaret Truman and Commodore Harry Manning Bridge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in a secluded corner of Mobile, Alabama, past train tracks, deserted lots, and a county jail, sits a treasure of American history: the SS United States. The country’s flagship ocean liner, once proudly painted red, white, and blue, is now faded and marred by rust. Today, rather than sailing the silver swell of Atlantic waves, it sits in the flotsam-filled murk of the Mobile River. Yet even in the ship’s diminished state, I was awestruck by the sheer force of her towering presence when I paid her a visit on a sticky August afternoon. I wondered: What life remained in the SS United States yet?

A view of the SS United States from above.

At nearly 1,000 feet long, the SS United States has always occupied a world of superlatives. When she was built in the early 1950s, she was the largest ocean liner ever constructed entirely in the United States, measuring a cool 100 feet longer than the RMS Titanic and boasting five more decks than the doomed British passenger liner. To this day, SS United States still holds the record for the fastest transatlantic crossing by an ocean liner, made on her maiden voyage in July 1952 when she tore from Newly introduced York City to the United Kingdom in just 3 days, 10 hours, and 40 minutes. She regularly hosted the biggest names of the time, from artistic celebrities like Marilyn Monroe, Salvador Dalí, and Marlon Brando, to former presidents and first ladies like Harry Truman, Dwight Eisenhower, and Eleanor Roosevelt.

Passengers on the maiden voyage included Margaret Truman and Commodore Harry Manning Bridge.

Sources indicate that those glory days did not last. In November 1969, the crew had just disembarked from the ship’s 400th voyage when they were abruptly informed that it had been their last. A perfect storm of affordable passenger jet travel, rising oil and labor costs, and the withdrawal of government subsidies had put the SS United States out of business after only 17 years of passenger travel. She has since spent nearly six decades bouncing from buyer to buyer, searching for a purpose.

Now, the storied liner at last has a newly introduced home and calling: She’s becoming the world’s largest artificial reef.

Sources indicate that on November 12, the SS United States will be sunk off the coast of Destin, Florida, where she will shelter dozens of species of fish and other marine life, and become a major destination for recreational divers and fishers. I had come to her current home in Alabama for a behind-the-scenes tour of her labyrinthine corridors and expansive decks—one of the last ever above water.

Alex Fogg, the natural resources chief for Destin-Fort Walton Beach tourism, and the mastermind behind the project, was my guide for the day. Despite the blanket-like heat, we both wore long pants, closed-toe shoes, and white safety helmets. “We are going to be on a ship that has holes that have been cut in the floor, and there’s things above your head,” Fogg warned me. “So just be aware of where you’re stepping.”.

In a recent development, with that, we walked up a narrow plank leading to a small, rusted steel door on the ship’s towering port side. The light inside was dim, and came only from the gaps where glass windows and portholes once stood. We marched up a narrow spiral staircase to a deck two floors above, where the first-class cabins once were. The doors and walls had long since been removed, but outlines of the floor plans still remained etched into the metal, as did shower and toilet drains, giving an idea of how the poshest passengers lived on board.

In a recent development, we climbed the remnants of a grand staircase, and reached a long indoor promenade deck that was once lined with floor-to-ceiling windows, but is was now exposedopen to the elements. The tour continued past empty lounges where copious martinis were no doubt served, and I imagined the ghosts of jazz bands past playing on now-hollowed-out stages. We passed the captain’s dining room, where the most elite guests took their meals, but now spiders were the only diners. On the bow, I took a photo for scale with the ship’s anchor—the largest I’d ever seen, resembling an ancient vertebra from some prehistoric leviathan. The tour wrapped up with a visit to the engine room, a jumble of pipes, catwalks and rails that were like a steampunk rendition of Chutes and Ladders.

It was surreal to imagine all of this, the entirety of the SS United States, soon underwater, given over to the crustaceans and fishes and sea turtles. Marine life will likely arrive within hours of the ship sinking, Fogg indicates, but it will probably take at least a year for the ecosystem to fully blossom.

Sources indicate that unlike other parts of Florida, the aquamarine waters off Destin-Fort Walton Beach lack an abundance of reef and other habitat that encourage a greater diversity and population of marine species. But artificial reefs can provide a substitute for these natural features. Thanks in part to Fogg’s leadership, more than 600 artificial reefs, ranging from small blocks of concrete to entire sunken ships, have already been installed in Destin-Fort Walton Beach since 2017, greatly boosting diving and fishing opportunities.

In a recent development, fogg had been looking for an iconic vessel to become the crown jewel of this program when he received a message from a contractor about the SS United States needing a new home. After Googling the ship, he realized it more than fit the bill. “I was like, ‘Man, I really want that,’” he told me. Despite the suitability of the ship for his needs, he had little idea of how complicated it would be to turn his vision into a reality.

Sources indicate that at the time, the ship was in Philadelphia, owned and cared for by a nonprofit organization called the SS United States Conservancy. Some conservancy officers and board members had family ties or personal histories with their group’s namesake vessel, however, and sinking it was, according to Fogg, “not their number one choice.”.

Board member Warren Jones, for example, was a passenger in 1961 and 1962. “It was just so unforgettable, sailing past the Statue of Liberty and just thinking, ‘Wow, we are going out to sea!’” Jones told me. He was just eight years old at the time of his sailings, but he still vividly remembers his time on board, including running through the black-and-silver first-class ballroom with his sister, watching Disney movies in the theater, and almost getting blown overboard by the North Atlantic wind.

Industry observers note that jones, like others at the conservancy, originally hoped to find a developer who would refurbish the ship. But after various deals fell through—including one to turn her into a recreational destination at Pier 76 in Manhattan—their choices began to narrow. Fogg and his colleagues’ solution was much better than the alternatives, Jones admitted: “She’s not being scrapped, and she’s not just deteriorating at some pier somewhere.” Still, he remarked, “bittersweet is the best way to describe my feelings.”.

According to recent reports, purchasing the ship from the conservancy was only the first step. Getting her out of Philadelphia was another major feat, requiring a detailed survey and much negotiation with the Coast Guard. After finally arriving in Mobile in March 2025, the ship began an extensive environmental remediation process. The asbestos walls that once made up the cabins had already been removed years before, but a specialized team still had to spend the better part of a year cleaning out around 120 fuel tanks, scraping off loose paint, carting away debris, ripping out the old ventilation system, and responsibly disposing of toxic materials.

Recent findings suggest that the ship’s dozen elevators were also removed, in part because they were covered in grease, but also to aid in sinking the ship efficiently, by opening up a path for the air to escape. “When you deploy a vessel, you want the air to get out very promptly and the water to get in very quickly,” Fogg said. “If not, it’ll weeble-wobble and could potentially end up on its side.”.

Industry observers note that the sinking will be carried out not with explosives, as was the past norm, but by opening valves connected to huge, disconnected boiler pipes to allow water to flood in. A naval architect on the project calculated that the ship will be fully submerged within 45 minutes after these valves are opened. Fogg and a few others will dive the wreck that very day to survey how she settled and remove mounted IMAX cameras that will capture video of the sinking. By the next day, according to Fogg, eager recreational divers will arrive.

Sources indicate that above the waterline, visitor center exhibits and a land-based museum will also soon keep the ship’s legacy alive, filled with artifacts and stories that the conservancy has carefully preserved. Jones noted he takes comfort in the truth that, once again, the SS United States will be a source of wonder and delight for the public. Of his time on board, he said, “It was a real feeling of joy. People were just so happy to be there.”.

#97. Don’t Visit Ko Lipe

📅 23 Feb 2026 • ⏱️ 7 min read (1489 words)
General 🌐 Nomadicmatt

Don’t Visit Ko Lipe

📅 23 Feb 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read | Source: Nomadicmatt

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, after 19 years, I finally went back to Ko Lipe, the Thai island I spent close to a month on in 2006.
  • It has been revealed that there was much to do here but that was the point.
  • It was paradise – and a place a lot of people got stuck.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, after 19 years, I finally went back to Ko Lipe, the Thai island I spent close to a month on in 2006. Back then, it was one of those super off-the-beaten-path destinations that few but the most intrepid travelers visited, where electricity only ran a few hours a day, basic bungalows right on the beach cost something like $2 USD, and there really was a last boat for the season.

It has been revealed that there was much to do here but that was the point. You hung out on the beach, read a book, went snorkeling, went back to the beach, drank beers at the one beach bar on the island, rotated meals between the five restaurants there, and went to bed early.

It was paradise – and a place a lot of people got stuck. Days easily turned into weeks here.

According to recent reports, if you asked me what the highlight of all my travels was, I would be the time I spent on Ko Lipe. I made incredible friends, lounged around, got to know the locals, learned a bit of Thai, and, overall, lived that idyllic backpacker life we all dream about.

Sources indicate that over the years, I’ve avoided going back to Ko Lipe because the memory of my time there is so strong that I didn’t want to ruin it. Any re-visit would simply be trying to recreated a magic that couldn’t be recreated because the people that it special wouldn’t be there. I’d be chasing travel ghosts. And, since I know my sleepy paradise has been developed greatly over the years, I was also too afraid seeing that would make me sad.

According to recent reports, tourism in Thailand tends toward the unsustainable. No island really develops in a good way. It’s all build, build, build.

And I didn’t want to see my Ko Lipe like that.

But as I was planning my recent trip through Southeast Asia, returning to Ko Lipe made sense. I was heading down the Indian Ocean side of Thailand on my way into Malaysia and I’d pass by it.

And, since I was looking for a lively place for Newly introduced Year’s Eve, it seemed liked the best choice. I knew there would be travelers there and there were no other nearby islands that would work, especially since Ko Lipe has a boat to Langkawi, which was my next stop.

And I’m sad to report that Ko Lipe took the Ko Phi Phi model of tourism and is now extremely overdeveloped.

Most of the island is now paved over, the old dirt footpaths having become concrete for the cars and construction trucks. Swaths of palm trees are now the sites of high-end resorts with pools (on an island with no natural water supply). Construction of more resorts continues at a fast pace. The coral around the island is dying, a victim of all the boats, anchors, pollution, and overfishing. Beaches are now lined with boats, their exhaust spilling into the ocean, leaving a shiny film you can see as you swim. And the restaurants cater to tourists looking for bad Western food, not great Thai cuisine.

The island’s boom has displaced many locals, who were forced to sell to mainland developers, and much of the island’s workforce is now from the mainland. They see little of the benefits this tourism boom.

So lies Ko Lipe, another victim of Thailand’s all too common overdevelopment and exploitation of limited resources.

According to recent reports, I met lots of people there who loved the island. If it’s your first time, I can see why you would love it. After all, the area is postcard perfect, the water is perfectly an azure blue, the sand is a beautiful white, and since you’re surrounded by a national park, a lot of tours take you to some secluded islands.

And, in comparison to Ko Phi Phi, Krabi, or Phuket, it is less developed so I can’t fault someone stepping here for the first time going “wow!”.

But, as I reflect on the island and its overdevelopment, I have come to the same conclusion I have about Ko Phi Phi: people shouldn’t visit.

I’m not against growth, but I’m against this kind of growth. It’s not sustainably managed and going there will only tax the island’s limited resources even further. You can’t put the genie back in the bottle and no local is going to say “sure, I’ll stay broke so you can an idealized vision of the world.”.

And, with so many other islands to visit that are well managed (Ko Lanta, Ko Jum, and Ko Mook, to name three nearby), I think you should skip Ko Lipe.

A visit there will only make things worse.

Industry observers note that it pains me to say that, because it was such a beautiful place, and my original visit had a huge impact on my life. But if we’re going to be good stewards and travelers, sometimes you just have to say enough is enough.

And Ko Lipe is a place where enough is enough.

Go somewhere else that is better managed.

Riding elephants in Thailand went away when consumers became more conscious of it. Eco lodges got major because of consumers. Overtourism is talked about by consumers as much as it is by locals.

Maybe if enough people start to do something, Ko Lipe will change.

But, at the very least, by not going you are at least no contributing to the problem.

#96. How Many Crew Members Does It Take To Fly A KC-135 Stratotanker?

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12 min read (2365 words)
General 🌐 Simpleflying

How Many Crew Members Does It Take To Fly A KC-135 Stratotanker?

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read | Source: Simpleflying

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that first flown in 1956, the Boeing KC-135 Stratotanker has spent decades refueling US military aircraft in flight.
  • It has been revealed that the KC-135's crew arrangement is not quite as straightforward as it might seem.
  • Industry observers note that for a normal refueling mission, according to the US Air Force's KC-135 fact sheet, the standard crew is three.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that first flown in 1956, the Boeing KC-135 Stratotanker has spent decades refueling US military aircraft in flight. Despite its age, it remains a major part of the United States Air Force's tanker fleet, supporting fighters, bombers, and other aircraft on missions around the world. But how many people does it actually take to operate an aircraft responsible for such an important job? The answer raises some interesting questions about how the Stratotanker was designed and how its crew responsibilities have changed over the years.

It has been revealed that the KC-135's crew arrangement is not quite as straightforward as it might seem. Its refueling missions require close coordination between the cockpit crew and the operator responsible for transferring fuel, while other missions can bring additional personnel aboard. Its history also raises questions about why it differs from commercial aircraft of the same era and how its crew compares with that of the newer KC-46 Pegasus. Looking at these differences helps explain how the Stratotanker has continued to serve for so many decades.

Industry observers note that for a normal refueling mission, according to the US Air Force's KC-135 fact sheet, the standard crew is three. The KC-135R and KC-135T normally operate with a three-person crew: a pilot, a copilot, and a boom operator. The two pilots occupy the cockpit, while the boom operator works at the rear of the aircraft, controlling the flying boom used to transfer fuel to the receiving aircraft. The National Museum of the US Air Force confirms the same crew number for the KC-135R. The more interesting question is how those three people divide the work.

According to recent reports, the workload is substantial. The Air Force fact sheet gives the Stratotanker a maximum takeoff weight of 322,500 pounds (146,285 kg), with up to 200,000 pounds (90,719 kg) of transfer fuel and, depending on configuration, as much as 83,000 pounds (37,648 kg) of cargo. The aircraft carries all of that on a wingspan of 130 feet, 10 inches (39.88 meters), yet the normal crew is still small enough to sit around a kitchen table.

It has been revealed that that was not always the case. Early KC-135s carried four people, with a navigator joining the two pilots and boom operator, before advances in navigation and avionics removed that position from the standard crew. The aircraft has nevertheless remained in service for decades. According to Simple Flying, the Air Force still operates roughly 396 Stratotankers across active-duty wings, the Air National Guard and the Air Force Reserve.

According to recent reports, more recent Air Force figures cited by the Government Accountability Office put the fleet at 373 aircraft as of early March 2026, before accounting for the losses and damage sustained during Operation Epic Fury against Iran. The Congressional Research Service later listed seven KC-135s as lost or damaged during the conflict. With hundreds of Stratotankers still in the inventory and the basic crew arrangement remaining central to their operation, the obvious next question is what each crew member is actually responsible for.

Sources indicate that the three-person crew arrangement makes more sense once the KC-135's refueling system comes into view. Aerial refueling requires two aircraft to maintain close formation while a rigid boom connects them in flight. The Air Force lists the KC-135's maximum speed at 530 miles per hour (853 km/h) at 30,000 feet (9,144 meters), although fuel transfer takes place at speeds appropriate to the aircraft involved. The receiving jet moves into position below and behind the tanker, the boom extends, and the final connection is made from the rear of the Stratotanker.

According to recent reports, each crew member has a specific responsibility. The pilot flies the tanker and maintains a stable flight path, while the copilot shares flying duties, handles communications and checklists, and monitors aircraft systems. At the back, the boom operator, an enlisted airman, controls the boom and guides its nozzle into the receiving aircraft. The National Museum of the US Air Force explains that the operator uses small wing-like control surfaces called ruddervators to steer the boom into position. Working from a prone position and looking through a window, the operator effectively flies the boom itself. The system can transfer nearly all the KC-135's usable fuel, while a drogue attachment can be fitted to support aircraft equipped with refueling probes. The arrangement has proved capable of some extraordinary missions.

The museum's KC-135R earned the Mackay Trophy for a sortie flown on May 31, 1967, after a Navy pilot was shot down in Southeast Asia and a rescue operation ran into fuel difficulties. Two US Navy Douglas KA-3 Skywarriors kept a pair of Vought F-8 Crusaders airborne, but both the tankers and the fighters were running low on fuel. The KC-135 crew began refueling the KA-3s while continuing to pass fuel to the F-8s. In effect, one tanker was refueling another tanker that was simultaneously refueling a fighter. The KC-135 subsequently provided additional fuel to two McDonnell Douglas F-4 Phantom fighters on its way to an alternative landing base.

Interestingly, although the KC-135 could operate with a basic crew of three, the aircraft involved in this award-winning mission carried four. Its crew consisted of Major John H. Casteel, aircraft commander; Captain Richard L. Trail, copilot; Captain Dean L. Hoar, navigator; and Master Sergeant Nathan C. Campbell, boom operator. This historical example illustrates the distinction between the aircraft's earlier four-person arrangement and its modern standard crew. The additional crew member was a navigator, not a flight engineer.

Here’s how the B-52’s crew works and why the United States Air Force wants fewer airmen.

It has been revealed that the navigator's presence on earlier KC-135 missions helps explain how the tanker's crew evolved over time, but it also highlights a more fundamental difference between the aircraft and its civilian contemporaries: the absence of a dedicated flight engineer. The tanker was developed alongside the Boeing 707, and many airliners of the period used a third cockpit crewmember to monitor engines and systems. Yet Air Force records for the KC-135 identify pilots, a boom operator and, on earlier versions, a navigator.

Industry observers note that the absence of a flight engineer from the standard KC-135 crew does not mean the aircraft never employed one. In a 2017 Air Force profile, Master Sgt. Robert Self was described as the service's last KC-135 flight engineer, following a career that included assignments on specialized NKC-135 and KC-135 aircraft used for testing and support programs. His responsibilities included operating the fuel panel, monitoring aircraft systems and advising the pilots. He also recalled that earlier KC-135 configurations had carried both flight engineers and navigators, positions that gradually disappeared as onboard computers and avionics became more capable.

Two pilots were always intended to occupy the front seats, with the boom operator handling refueling from the rear. Then the avionics changed. As reported by the National Guard in a story about Iowa's 185th, PACER CRAG brought compass, radar, and GPS improvements to the fleet by the early 2000s, while modern GPS removed the need for the navigator on standard missions. GlobalSecurity's overview of the program likewise notes that the commercial off-the-shelf upgrade eliminated the navigator requirement on most missions. The Simple Flying report mentioned earlier adds that digital flight decks and enhanced autopilots have further reduced the workload.

It has been revealed that the tradeoff is workload. A base spokesman at Fairchild told the Spokane Journal that, while the upgrades were arriving,it basically meant more responsibility for the pilot and copilot. Navigation functions moved into the avionics, while some tasks previously handled by another crew member became part of the cockpit workload. This distinction is vital when comparing the KC-135 with the Boeing KC-46, which was designed from the outset around a very different refueling station and a more modern approach to crew responsibilities.

The easiest way to see the difference is to look at the boom operator. On the KC-135, that person works at the rear of the aircraft and looks outside through a window. On the KC-46 Pegasus, there is no comparable window to look through. According to Air Mobility Command's KC-46A fact sheet, the Pegasus uses a fly-by-wire refueling boom and gives its Air Refueling Operator panoramic displays with wingtip-to-wingtip situational awareness. From that station, the operator controls the boom, centerline drogue, and wing aerial refueling pods.

It has been revealed that the screen-based system was intended to offer advantages, but it also created problems that required a major redesign. The same fact sheet says that the Air Force and Boeing agreed in April 2020 on the final Remote Vision System design, known as RVS 2.0, after deficiencies had affected safe and effective refueling. The matter has not disappeared completely: as Simple Flying reported, the Pegasus still has refueling limitations with some US Air Force aircraft, including the FairchildA-10 Warthog, while Boeing works on boom and vision-system fixes. The KC-135's window may look primitive alongside the KC-46's cameras, but it also offers a remarkably direct view of the aircraft being refueled.

It has been revealed that the contrast does not mean the KC-135 is about to disappear. According to Simple Flying, the Air Force originally planned to field 179 KC-46s, but that figure has since grown substantially. The current program calls for 263 Pegasus tankers, almost 100 more than the original requirement, as the service looks to replace much of its aging KC-135 fleet. As of early March 2026, the Air Force had 373 KC-135s and 103 KC-46As in its inventory, according to the Government Accountability Office. The Pegasus is the newer design, but the Stratotanker remains a major part of the force and is being kept in service for decades longer than originally intended. That creates an important question about the three-person crew: is it sufficient for every mission the aging tanker is now being asked to perform?

Industry observers note that how many crew members does the V-22 Osprey need? The answer depends on the military service, the mission, and the demands of each variant.

The three-person crew is a starting point, not a fixed rule. The Air Force fact sheet notes that some missions require a navigator and that only a limited number of navigator suites are available for those specialized tasks. It is an uncommon arrangement today, but it shows why the published crew number needs a little context: the KC-135's staffing changes with the mission.

It has been revealed that aeromedical evacuation is the clearest example. The KC-135 can carry litter and ambulatory patients on patient support pallets, and the fact sheet says an aeromedical evacuation mission adds a basic medical crew of five: two flight nurses and three medical technicians. That number can change according to the patients being carried. In the basic configuration described by the Air Force, a hospital mission can therefore put eight crew members aboard before the patients themselves are counted.

For aeromedical evacuation, the KC-135's cargo compartment can be fitted with a stanchion litter system, allowing patients to travel on a secured litter rather than ordinary passenger seats. The system must be assembled and attached inside the aircraft by support personnel, while the medical team brings the equipment needed to monitor and care for patients during flight.

Sources indicate that another issue that is harder to solve with crew changes is age. The last KC-135 was delivered in 1965, so even the newest aircraft are now decades old. As reported by ExecutiveBiz, SNC has assembled a team with BAE Systems, Collins Aerospace and GE Aerospace to pursue the Air Force's KC-135 Center Console Refresh, a program aimed at replacing aging fuel-system equipment, flight displays and computing architecture. SNC confirmed the consortium in November 2026.

BAE would design the fuel management system to reduce pilot workload; Collins, which has supplied KC-135 avionics for more than three decades, would add fresh displays and computers built on an open architecture; and GE Aerospace would contribute avionics already flying on the KC-46 and Lockheed C-130 Hercules. The proposal also includes autothrottle capability, with performance projected from July 2028 through June 2038 and the award still anticipated. In other words, the same aircraft that learned to do without a navigator decades ago may soon get another set of tools designed to make the remaining crew's jobs easier.

The standard KC-135 Stratotanker crew consists of three people: a pilot, a copilot, and a boom operator. Earlier configurations commonly included a fourth crew member, a navigator, whose position gradually disappeared as navigation systems and avionics improved. Specialized missions can still require additional personnel, while aeromedical evacuation typically adds five medical crew members to the basic crew. Flight engineers also served aboard certain specialized KC-135 aircraft, but they were not part of the standard operational crew. The result is an aircraft that has retained its essential three-person operating arrangement while adapting to decades of technological change.

That makes the boom operator the most distinctive member of the crew. From the rear of the tanker, one person is responsible for the final connection between two aircraft moving in formation, doing it through a window that has been part of the KC-135's design for generations. The KC-46 approaches the same task from the opposite direction, replacing that view with cameras and displays. The basic mission has barely changed; the way the crew carries it out has.

According to recent reports, the KC-135's story is not yet finished simply because the KC-46 is entering the force. Looking ahead, Air & Space Forces Magazine reports that the Air Force plans to keep the KC-135 until at least 2050, even as it considers a bridge tanker and a future Next-Generation Air-Refueling System. If the cockpit refresh moves forward, the old tanker could receive a substantially modernized flight deck under the program's 2028 to 2038 timeline. For a design that first flew in the 1950s, the next chapter may be less about adding people and more about giving the same three-person crew better tools for the job.

#93. Industry News: Singapore Airlines Reconsiders Upcoming Business Class Seat Design After Backlash

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6 min read (1228 words)
General 🌐 Onemileatatime

Industry News: Singapore Airlines Reconsiders Upcoming Business Class Seat Design After Backlash

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read | Source: Onemileatatime

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Last week, Singapore Airlines unveiled all-upcoming cabins, with the most exciting developments being a new first class and new business class.
  • While the airline vehemently defended the color choices for several days, it seems that they’re at least now reconsidering it, though it remains to be seen if it’s too late to make a change….
  • In a recent development, on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, Singapore Airlines CEO Goh Choon Phong had a town hall with employees, as reported by The Business Times.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last week, Singapore Airlines unveiled all-upcoming cabins, with the most exciting developments being a new first class and new business class. The new cabins look great (nothing revolutionary, but a huge improvement), with one exception — the new business class seat colors. Not only do they look cheap, but they just seem completely mismatched to the rest of the cabin.

While the airline vehemently defended the color choices for several days, it seems that they’re at least now reconsidering it, though it remains to be seen if it’s too late to make a change….

In a recent development, on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, Singapore Airlines CEO Goh Choon Phong had a town hall with employees, as reported by The Business Times. During this, he was asked about the negative feedback the airline has received about the newly introduced business class seat design.

Sources indicate that in response to this, he reportedly mentioned “we’ll look at it, we’ll see what’s feasible.” So that signals some willingness to make changes, though admittedly with how far out seats are ordered, that’s not necessarily so straightforward, so I wouldn’t count on anything happening. He did, however, emphasize that customers will come to like the seats after experiencing its comforts for themselves.

At the town hall, Singapore Airlines Chief Commercial Officer Lee Lik Hsin stated this was a good learning point for the airline, but indicated that he hopes customers will mind the colors less after experiencing the seats. He also reportedly said “I suppose, you know, it’s the 80-20 rule, you can’t please them all.”.

At the time of launch, Singapore Airlines VP of Product Experience, Ong Wah Li, explained the latest design was in response to customer feedback, and described it as “modern, fresh, yet elegant and refined, that’s suited to business travel.”.

BMW Designworks was behind the design of the cabin, and CEO Julia de Bono defended the color choices at the launch event, describing them as “more refreshing and more progressive.” As she viewed it, “what I see when I look at it, it’s definitely like a nice suit, with the white and the metal really popping out, you know, it’s more like a suit with a sneaker, so a bit more modern and fresh.”.

Industry observers note that to state the obvious, the trim and finishes on a latest business class seat are hardly the most pressing issues facing the world. However, Singapore Airlines prides itself in being perhaps the most detail oriented airline in the world, because management has an obsessive attention to even the smallest things.

So I can’t help but be a bit confused by all of this:.

It also just feels to me like the mandate for the design of this product was off, as shared by the CEO of BMW Designworks. Premium travel demand is through the roof, and a lot of people in premium cabins aren’t traveling for business. For that matter, these cabins will be operating the world’s longest flights, so this isn’t a case of a business traveler hopping on a plane in a suit, and going straight to a meeting (at least that doesn’t make up a meaningful percentage of the traffic here).

It has been revealed that is “suit with a sneaker” really the vibe you want to go for with a latest business class product that’s on an airline that’s known for its incredible warmth? It’s almost like the airline views warmth and modernity as being at odds with one another, which I don’t at all agree with.

For example, reader Sam asked AI to take the new seat, but preserve the old color concept, and below is what it spit out.

That looks so much more on brand for Singapore Airlines than what the airline actually arrived at.

I would’ve loved to be a fly on the wall when this design was finalized. Was everyone immediately onboard with this, and thought it looked great? Or was there some skepticism, but someone said “trust me, people will love this, this is what a modern cabin looks like?”.

I just don’t understand how you can commit to investing in a project that costs billions of dollars, reportedly get feedback from hundreds of customers, and still end up so far off the pulse of public sentiment.

Sources indicate that last week, Singapore Airlines unveiled its new cabins, which is an exciting development. Everything looked pretty great, except the new business class seat finishes, which seem terribly mismatched to the brand. The airline claimed it wanted something modern and progressive, but I’m not sure “suit with sneakers” is really the aesthetic that the public wanted (or that the chosen finishes actually reflect that).

Singapore Airlines leadership claims it’s now looking into possibly updating finishes, but I wouldn’t count on anything coming of that, given how far along this is.

What do you make of this Singapore Airlines business class design fiasco? And I’m still waiting for someone to please tell me that they love the design, and think it’s great!

#92. Tech Report: 15 Hotels With Actually Luxurious Indoor Pools

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14 min read (2767 words)
General 🌐 Cntraveler

Tech Report: 15 Hotels With Actually Luxurious Indoor Pools

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read | Source: Cntraveler

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s hard to nail an indoor pool—they can very easily veer into athletic club territory, where the smell of chlorine is inescapable, and every splash seems to elicit an unwanted echo.
  • Location: Lake Louise, CanadaThe pool: A heated pool with an adjacent steam room, featuring views of Lake Louise.
  • Recent findings suggest that nestled in Alberta’s Banff National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, the Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise is surrounded by the best of nature.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s hard to nail an indoor pool—they can very easily veer into athletic club territory, where the smell of chlorine is inescapable, and every splash seems to elicit an unwanted echo. Outdoor pools, with their trompe l’oeil effects and decadent sun loungers, often get most of the credit, but some of their indoor counterparts can pull off even better architectural indicates. From thermal baths powered by hot springs to top-level tanks with skyline views, the indoor pools on this list are nothing short of spectacular—not to mention, they can be enjoyed year-round, so you won’t miss out when it rains in New York or Paris. Far from your YMCA, these pools have design details you’ll swoon over: skylights, floor-to-ceiling windows, vaulted ceilings, mosaic tiling, and more. Yes, these hotels are worth booking for the awe-inspiring swims alone. Read on for the best indoor pools at hotels around the world, spanning Mexico to Vietnam.

Location: Lake Louise, CanadaThe pool: A heated pool with an adjacent steam room, featuring views of Lake Louise.

Recent findings suggest that nestled in Alberta’s Banff National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, the Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise is surrounded by the best of nature. Clear blue skies, mountain peaks, the Victoria Glacier, and the emerald-colored Lake Louise create a storybook backdrop that’s worth traveling for. One of the newest and most exciting additions to the Fairmont is the 2025 opening of Basin Glacial Waters, an all-sensory thermal bathing facility that fuses nature and science to offer its guests the ultimate indoor-outdoor wellness experience. From cold plunges and steam rooms to indoor-outdoor thermal pools with some of the best views that Lake Louise has to offer, there are restorative options for every individual’s needs. White-glove service, a cutting-edge wellness space, and once-in-a-lifetime vistas await. —Meaghan Kenny.

Location: Upcoming York City, New YorkThe pool: A 65-foot, heated, Japanese-inspired sanctuary.

It has been revealed that in the four decades since Aman was founded and its first property opened its doors in Phuket, the brand has come to represent a certain kind of experience for a certain kind of traveler: discreet, expansive, and intimate, with a full-bodied approach to wellness (one of the best spas in New York) and an almost chameleon-like ability to adapt to the surrounding landscape. Aman New York is the brand’s very first urban outpost in the United States and only its second urban property in the world after Aman Tokyo. The Beaux Arts landmark was carefully renovated by Belgian designer Jean-Michel Gathy of Denniston Architects; the space dazzles with a 7,000-square-foot outdoor terrace, a spa and wellness center spread over three floors, and serene guest suites (each with its own fireplace). You can swim laps in the magnificent 65-foot pool, or post up on one of the poolside chaises, which are interspersed with fireplaces. —Betsy Blumenthal.

Location: Chicago, IllinoisThe pool: A heated pool with floor-to-ceiling windows offering views of Lake Michigan and the Chicago River.

When the undulating tower that is the St. Regis opened in 2020, it became the tallest building in the world by a female architect (Jeanne Gang)—a title it still holds. And the wait was worth it: Glorious city, lake, and river views; a stellar hotel gym; two restaurants; and a world-class spa with an indoor pool and outdoor terrace bring a newly introduced dimension to urban luxury. Though the tower sits right above the Chicago River, the space between its circular driveway and Lake Michigan is a very posh (and quiet) residential area called Lakeshore East. The wellness floor includes a 12,000-square-foot spa and boasts an athletic club with a full fleet of state-of-the-art equipment, daily and group fitness classes, plus a dedicated Pilates reformer studio. —Heidi Mitchell.

Location: Mexico City, MexicoThe pool: A heated saltwater pool on the 38th floor, adjacent to the Cityzen Rooftop Bar.

The Sofitel Mexico City Reforma is a contemporary oasis to both imbibe and reset along Mexico City’s most enigmatic avenue. The property features 275 guest rooms, of which 56 are suites—for something truly special, book the Imperial Suite, which features floor-to-ceiling windows that look out onto the iconic Angel of Independence monument. The expansive urban spa (probably the best in the entire city) has hot and cold dipping tubs, both a steam and sauna room, and—best of all—a heated indoor pool, set one floor below the spa on the 38th level, where you can relax post-treatment with an unmatched view of Mexico City. But the real star of the property is Cityzen, a rooftop restaurant and cocktail bar that offers the perfect perch to view the city from above. —Michaela Trimble.

Location: Torres del Paine National Park, ChileThe pool: A glass-fronted, heated indoor infinity pool located within the Uma Spa.

According to recent reports, tinged red at dawn, the granite towers of Torres del Paine are a blazing centerpiece in Chile’s premier national park. But no view compares to the scene that greets guests from their bed at this exquisitely crafted lodge. Barely visible along the skyline, the lakeside building sinks comfortably into the landscape, giving all rooms a view onto the soaring peaks. Light pours through glass walls to illuminate a panoramic restaurant and spa with a heated indoor infinity pool, complete with a hydro-massage and water jets—watch the natural towers play hide-and-seek as clouds breeze by, and keep an eye out for guanacos and rheas, which come close to the lodge. Far from the crowd-clogged trails, this coolly unassuming property invites endless possibilities at the bottom of the world. —Sarah Marshall.

Location: Cadenabbia, ItalyThe pool: Part of the Longevity Spa, an indoor vitality pool featuring floor-to-ceiling views of Lake Como.

Recent findings suggest that the Lake Como Edition merges palatial grandeur with the Edition group’s signature cutting-edge design. In a destination saturated with old-school addresses, this hotel might be exactly what Italy’s grandest lake needs to inject a dose of contemporary cool. Located just over an hour’s drive from Milan airport, the Lake Como Edition is housed within a restored 19th-century palazzo, and sits on the lake’s western shore in the small but charming village of Cadenabbia, just steps from the water’s edge. Across the glassy expanse, postcard-perfect Bellagio stretches into view, as ferries glide hypnotically back and forth between the shores. A standout feature of the hotel is the Longevity Spa: Facilities include an indoor pool, steam room, herbal sauna, and plunge pools, all set within a deeply tranquil space. Following a meticulous four-year renovation that was completed in 2026, creative directors Kirstin Bailey and Paul Haslhofer have carefully preserved the building’s historic bones while introducing a more contemporary aesthetic.—Lucy Bruton.

Location: Bad Ragaz, SwitzerlandThe pool: A 19th-century thermal pool fed by the Tamina Gorge waters.

Industry observers note that in 1242, a bird hunter in the Tamina Gorge discovered a pure hot spring with healing minerals and a consistently toasty temperature of 97 degrees. Visitors have been traveling here to take advantage of the thermal water’s healing properties ever since. Today, that “blue gold” is one of many draws of Grand Resort Bad Ragaz in eastern Switzerland, about an hour’s drive from Zurich. Comprising four interconnected hotels, the resort offers guests two thermal spas, saunas, steam rooms, and hammams, as well as its signature NewYou Method: A holistic, evidence-based approach that uses the latest findings in medicine and wellness to help each individual. For dining options, you’ll find at least six Michelin stars among the seven restaurants, including the three-Michelin-starred Sven Wassmer Memories. There, Chef Wassmer uses the Alpine region as his seasonal pantry. —Caitlin Gunther.

Location: Berlin, GermanyThe pool: A 65-foot-long indoor pool, part of a 19th-century bathhouse.

Hotel Oderberger's setting is one of the most splendid in Berlin: It's inside Prenzlauer Berg's landmarked 19th-century Stadtbad Oderberger, a public bathhouse designed by architect Ludwig Hoffmann, who also created the city’s iconic Pergamon Museum. The conversion to a boutique hotel preserved many of the grand building’s original details, most notably the 65-foot-long indoor pool, set beneath a magnificent vaulted stone ceiling and surrounded by massive arched columns and huge, church-like windows. It's the first thing you see when you enter the lobby, and it definitely impresses. The 72 rooms are all unique in layout, and the modern design incorporates historic details in a clever way: Original numbered wood doors from the bathing cabins, now glassed in, live on as bathroom doors. Go for the cool historical details and great location in the heart of buzzy Prenzlauer Berg. —Jennifer Ceaser.

Location: Furnas, PortugalThe pool: A thermal spring pool fed by heated volcanic waters.

Recent findings suggest that octant Furnas offers a calming, restorative escape from the already serene São Miguel, the largest island of the Azores archipelago. You’ll feel taken care of at every moment, and the scenery is some of the most beautiful you’ll ever lay eyes on. It occupies the structure that was once the old Furnas Thermal Center, and while the Furnas volcano last erupted in 1630, the geothermal activity remains around both the hotel and the entire town of Furnas. That means the indoor pool is filled with naturally heated thermal water, and yes, one dip will melt all your troubles away. The hotel boasts 54 rooms of various sizes with something for parties of every size; every room is spacious, incorporating small details like Marshall speakers, and comes with robes, slippers, and sun hats for enjoying the pools. The central meeting place of the hotel is the signature restaurant À Terra, with its beautiful outdoor seating area, glass roof, and hanging plants. —Kate Kassin.

Location: Cádiz, SpainThe pool: Part of the on-site spa, a light-filled indoor pool overlooking the gardens of La Alcaidesa.

In a recent development, oku Andalusia brings the wabi-sabi cool of its Ibiza and Kos siblings to a sprawling beachfront resort on Cádiz’s quieter stretch of the Costa del Sol. Its 255 rooms and suites pair earthy minimalism with thoughtful design details; families and groups will particularly appreciate the impressive 72 suites, private-pool options, and four-bedroom villa. Not to mention there’s a world-class kids club and extensive activity programming for toddlers to teens. Yet adults aren’t forgotten: Two child-free pools, DJs, and wellness experiences create a grown-up counterpoint. Even if you’re not booked in for a treatment, make time for the spa’s indoor pool. It is an arch-filled architectural delight, and offers a serene contrast to the cool Balearic-house soundtrack of the main pools. Oku is that rare, family-friendly resort where couples and child-free guests can still enjoy a more grown-up experience. —Bridget Mills-Powell.

Location: Paris, FranceThe pool: Paris’s longest indoor pool, featuring handcrafted mosaics and digital depictions of the city skyline.

According to recent reports, skip the sleepy districts that house so many of Paris’s plush hotels, and book a private perch with a bird’s-eye view of the river and La Samaritaine as your fashion-forward neighbor. From a sophisticated suburban crowd to the “bobos” (bourgeois-bohème) of the right bank, every type of Parisian rubs shoulders with jet-setting guests in the convivial seventh-floor Art Deco brasserie-meets-cocktail bar, Le Tout-Paris. It’s the place to be seen before you escape to the subterranean spa or your room with a view. More than half of the 72 elegant rooms, 46 of which are suites, overlook the Seine. Tucked away below ground, the brightly lit spa, designed like a modern living room, is helmed by another member of the LVMH équipe and star of both Parisian couture and beauty: Christian Dior. The nearly 100‑foot pool is mentioned to be the city’s (and continent's) longest hotel pool; it’s designed by architect Peter Marino, situated under a mirrored ceiling, and surrounded by handcrafted mosaics by Michael Mayer and large-scale digital screens that create the effect of looking out at the Seine and Paris’s skyline. —Madison Flager.

Location: Oyama, JapanThe pool: A 59-foot-long, groundwater-fed pool with a view of Mount Fuji.

It has been revealed that practically every window, every sliding door, and every gap between the trees at Gora Kadan Fuji frames Japan’s most iconic peak, Mount Fuji. The mountain may be the star of the show here, but there’s a lot more to love when it’s shrouded in clouds. Gora Kadan Fuji’s 39 suites and three villas feature tatami, granite, paper, and cypress in a flawless blend of traditional Japanese design and contemporary comfort. Service, delivered by attentive staff in exquisite kimonos, is calm and caring. Breakfast is a succession of delicate, locally sourced morsels presented in pretty little dishes. Convivial dinners take place at the seven-seater counter of Kappo and at equally bijou Sushi Fuji Takumi, where seafood from nearby waters is transformed into seasonal nigiri. Guests soak neck-deep in communal and private onsen baths, filled from underground springs and snowmelt groundwater. The spa also has a 59-foot indoor pool with Fuji views and a small outdoor infinity pool, as well as a 24-hour gym. Gora Kadan Fuji is a place to return to in every season. —Nicola Chilton.

Location: Hanoi, VietnamThe pool: One of the largest pools you'll find at any hotel in Hanoi, with views of the skyline.

According to recent reports, the brainchild of architect Carlos Zapata, whose striking design draws inspiration from Vietnam's coastline and is meant to look like a dragon rising beside the water, the 450-room JW Marriott Hotel Hanoi has become one of the capital's defining business hotels. Its generous rooms and warm, intuitive service make it a rewarding retreat from the city's frenetic center, while standout dining—from the upscale French Grill to one of Hanoi's most expansive breakfast buffets—ensures there's plenty of reason to stay in. Suspended on the eighth floor beneath soaring floor-to-ceiling windows, the enormous indoor lap pool has the scale to make swimming a proper part of your stay rather than an afterthought. The surrounding wellness complex includes a well-equipped fitness center, sauna and steam rooms, and the Spa by JW. For travelers who value space, comfort, and a quieter setting, it's an easy recommendation. —Dan Q. Dao.

Location: Rabat, MoroccoThe pool: A year-round saltwater pool located within the spa.

A shiny, super-sized proposition from Four Seasons, this palatial hotel successfully incorporates beautiful Moroccan touches in the shared areas and sleek luxuries in the private spaces. This would be an ideal three- or four-night stop for a bit of sightseeing and a lot of pampering as part of a wider Moroccan tour, with Rabat being a serene introduction to what is a very colorful and frenetic country. The true headliner here is the spa, which has thorough and high-end treatments for every mood, with the opportunity to relax by the magnificent indoor pool afterwards (here, you can either get your laps in, or recline in a hot tub or steam room with bottled water or even Moroccan mint tea brought to your lounge chair). There’s an effortless blending of old and new, and a devotion to looking after the guest. —Matt Charlton.

Location: Melbourne, AustraliaThe pool: Located on the 64th floor, a heated infinity pool offering views of Melbourne’s skyline.

It has been revealed that when booking a stay down under, why not go to the very top? The Ritz-Carlton, Melbourne is Australia’s tallest hotel, housed in the top 17 floors of an 80-story building. The hotel’s unprecedented vantage point envelops guests in panoramic views of the city and the ocean lapping at Port Phillip Bay. If you find the views hard to pull away from, the in-house restaurant Atria, helmed by chef David Green, serves a seasonal five-course tasting menu for dinner, showcasing modern Australian cuisine at its freshest, with seats right at the window. With door-to-door valets and a Ritz Kids program where story time brings local Australian culture to life, the standard of service is as sky-high as the rooms. The chic, modern pool sits on the 64th floor, offering 24/7 access to water with an excellent view over the city.

According to recent reports, every hotel review on this list has been written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#91. United Bans AI Agents From Booking Flights For Customers

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2 min read (327 words)
AI & Tech 🌐 Airlinegeeks

United Bans AI Agents From Booking Flights For Customers

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read | Source: Airlinegeeks

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Citing concerns over data privacy and regulatory compliance, United mentioned Wednesday that it will block artificial intelligence bots from booking tickets on behalf of travelers.
  • airline, United will ban third-party AI from parts of its digital platforms and adjust its policies to prevent access via travel agencies and aggregators.
  • “Sharing account credentials with personal, third-party AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles,” the airline said in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Citing concerns over data privacy and regulatory compliance, United mentioned Wednesday that it will block artificial intelligence bots from booking tickets on behalf of travelers.

In the first such move by a U.S. airline, United will ban third-party AI from parts of its digital platforms and adjust its policies to prevent access via travel agencies and aggregators.

“Sharing account credentials with personal, third-party AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles,” the airline said in a statement.

In a recent development, the carrier also mentioned AI actions could violate FAA and Department of Transportation regulations. As an example, it cited the requirement that passengers confirm in person that their bags do not contain banned items, such as explosives.

According to recent reports, “As a result, United is taking steps to restrict access, directly within our digital platforms and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators, to prohibit use by unauthorized, third-party personal AI agents or assistants,” the statement continued. “This work includes updates to our booking, ticketing, and distribution policies.”.

In a recent development, united noted its stance is in line with companies in the banking and retail sectors. It is now “encourag[ing] others” to consider measures “that preserve the data and security of their customers and strengthen safety.”.

The airline stated it will update its Digital Trust Center to clarify the new restrictions.

#90. FAA Complications Nationwide Ground Stop For All US Flights

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5 min read (1067 words)
General 🌐 Simpleflying

FAA Complications Nationwide Ground Stop For All US Flights

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read | Source: Simpleflying

💡 Key Takeaways
  • * Last Updated: 9:15 PM EST November 13, 2026 by Channing Reid.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a rare nationwide ground stop at all US airports following communication failures affecting "multiple" air traffic control centers on Friday.
  • The exact cause of the ground stop is not yet known, but in a statement obtained by CNBC, the FAA stated, "communication issues" impacted air traffic control (ATC) centers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

* Last Updated: 9:15 PM EST November 13, 2026 by Channing Reid.

Recent findings suggest that the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a rare nationwide ground stop at all US airports following communication failures affecting "multiple" air traffic control centers on Friday. Citing extraordinary circumstances and safety concerns, the FAA has suspended all departures until further notice. International arrivals will be handled individually while technicians investigate the disruption.

The exact cause of the ground stop is not yet known, but in a statement obtained by CNBC, the FAA stated, "communication issues" impacted air traffic control (ATC) centers. Aviation watchdog JonNYC reported that the halt is not a “9/11 type of event”, which required flights to be forced to land at the closest airport available. Simple Flying's Flight Tracker captured ATC first communicating to pilots that all departures had been stopped.

The FAA lifted the nationwide ground stop at around 8:30 PM EST. All flights are allowed to resume, but some warn it could take days before airlines can restore their normal schedules.

Multiple sources have reported that the FAA's telecommunication infrastructure rebooted on Friday due to an upgrade to a private communications network that handles connections between the US' nationwide ATC system. Amid the reboot, the system crashed, resulting in a communications outage, according to CBS News Political Reporter Olivia Rinaldi. The system is reportedly operated by L3Harris – the same manufacturer responsible for the security overhaul of the Air Force One bridge Boeing 747-8.

According to recent reports, international flights are slowly resuming. According to Flightradar24, some eastbound transatlantic flights have been cleared to depart from airports across the Northeast.

The first flight from Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD) also departed around 7:15 PM EST. Despite the gradual resumption, the ground stop still remains in effect, meaning all domestic flights have not been cleared to resume.

There is no evidence that the Microsoft outage that affected millions of people worldwide on Thursday is related to the ground stop.

"Microsoft has no indication that the FAA nationwide ground stop is related to the recent service disruption," an FAA spokesperson noted in a statement obtained by NBC News.

It has been revealed that several major airports around the country have issued statements and notices to passengers about the ground stop. Officials at Miami International Airport (MIA) told passengers to stay away from the airport until they confirm their flight's status with their airline.

"MIA is coordinating closely with airlines and safety and security partners to monitor evolving conditions, support affected passengers, and maintain operational readiness," the airport noted in a statement. "Passengers are strongly urged NOT to come to MIA until they have confirmed directly with their airline that their flight is operating and have received updated travel instructions.".

Friday's ground stop is the second nationwide halt since the September 11, 2001 attacks. The last time such action occurred was in early 2023 when the FAA's Notice to Air Missions (NOTAM) system failed. All departures were grounded for about an hour and a half before resuming. Investigators mentioned that damage to a database file may have been the cause of the system failure.

Law enforcement officials say the ground stop is not the result of a cyberattack. However, personnel from the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) around the country are monitoring the situation, according to CNN.

Friday's ground halt comes on the heels of the FAA rolling out a fresh AI system to manage air traffic. While it is not clear that the telecommunications outage was directly related, the agency has been criticized for implementing the system.

It is known as the Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (SMART), and "analyzes airline schedules, weather, airport capacity, airspace conditions, and operational constraints to predict traffic airflows and identify potential conflicts before they occur," according to the FAA.

Recent findings suggest that all airborne aircraft were allowed to continue flying until further notice. According to FlightAware, more than 6,500 flights are currently halted.

The FAA confirmed that the ground stop was implemented "out of an abundance of caution" in a statement.

"There has been a temporary telecommunications outage - out of an abundance of caution all flights have been halted. Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis.".

Flightradar24 is reporting that more than 1,000 flights had already been canceled by 6:00 PM. Cirium data indicates that more than 11,000 flights were still set to depart across the US on Friday after the ground stop was put in place, so cancellations are expected to increase significantly as the evening progresses.

Ground controllers will also face growing difficulty as aircraft continue to land and none depart, putting pressure on already stressed infrastructure and increasingly scarce gate availability.

Sources indicate that we want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

Lots of aircraft look to be lined up on the taxiways.

Stuck on the field in Newark after landing but we’ve been told it may be several hours before we have a gate.

Check-in at DFW says no flights departing until 10 pm central at the earliest. Aircraft are landing though.

on flightradar it indicates SFO has had no takeoffs since 12:35 PST.

According to recent reports, we are.supposed to fly PHL-SFO Saturday morning but that's obviously not happening. The equipment's not leaving SFO tonight for one thing. Where do we go for advice and info on rescheduling and airline change fee waivers?

Recent findings suggest that so far only a few international flights have left IAD. At the time of the ground stop being confirmed, most flights were inbound anyway. So we expect to see many delays. Some flights have already canceled.

EDIT: More international flights are leaving. So far domestic flights are the ones being shafted the most.

sucks but everything is speculation until we know.

According to recent reports, landed MSP on my way to LAS. Found out about the ground stop just as we were deplaning. No information from the airlines - they don’t se to be getting anything from the FAA. For a while some flights were boarding but that has stopped.

Yesterday because of the storms in NYC, 17 planes went to BDL and one+ are coming as BOS gets backed up.
