General 🌐 Nomadicmatt

How the Antigravity 360 Drone Will Change Your Travels

📅 23 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read | Source: Nomadicmatt

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, drones are huge.
  • There’s lots of amazing brands out there but one that I think is super cool is the Antigravity A1.
  • I was sent one to use and want to share my experience and why I like this product so much.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, drones are huge. And, while there’s lots of restrictions around them, a lot of travelers take them on road because they produce some amazing sweeping aerial shots.

There’s lots of amazing brands out there but one that I think is super cool is the Antigravity A1. Released in late 2025, attempts to render the traditional gimbal obsolete for a vast segment of creators. By leveraging a dual-lens 360-degree capture system, the A1 records everything in every direction simultaneously. The result is a “fly now, frame later” experience that feels less like piloting a drone and more like directing a virtual camera in a pre-recorded digital environment.

I was sent one to use and want to share my experience and why I like this product so much.

In a recent development, what make’s Antigravity 360’s so special is the two lenses. Most drones feature a single lens that points forward. However, the A1 features two ultra-wide-angle lenses positioned on the top and bottom of the central fuselage that each captures a 200-degree field of view. When those images are combines, they overlap to create a seamless 360-degree sphere.

And, in the final exported footage, the drone itself is digitally removed, creating the illusion of a camera floating in mid-air with no visible means of support.

In a recent development, the sensors themselves are 1/1.28-inch CMOS units. While smaller than the 1-inch sensors found on some “Pro” level photography drones, they are massive compared to typical 360 action cameras. This allows for significantly better low-light performance and a higher dynamic range, capturing details in the highlights and shadows that would typically be lost in the harsh contrast of a midday sun.

Most countries require drones weighing 250 grams or more to be registered and subject to stricter flight rules. Antigravity clearly understood the importance of this threshold because they made the A1 to weigh exactly 249 grams with its standard battery meaning it’s not considered a commercial drone so you don’t have to register it.

Recent findings suggest that and the drone feels remarkably sturdy. It utilizes a high-grade carbon-fiber-reinforced polymer that offers a better strength-to-weight ratio than the standard ABS plastic found in cheaper models. The folding mechanism is satisfyingly tactile, clicking into place with a precision that suggests long-term durability. When folded, the drone is roughly the size of a large smartphone, though about three times as thick.

According to recent reports, the Vision Goggles: These are sleek, lightweight, and feature dual 4K micro-OLED displays with a 120Hz refresh rate. The latency is nearly non-existent and they have integrated head tracking. Because the drone is recording in 360 degrees, you aren’t limited to seeing what is in front of the drone. When you turn your head to the left, the goggle feed pans to the left. If you look down, you see the ground passing beneath you. This provides a sense of presence and spatial awareness that is simply impossible with a traditional fixed-camera drone.

The drone uses a single-handed motion controller. You point the controller where you want to go and pull the trigger to accelerate. Tilt your wrist left to bank, or raise the nose of the controller to climb. It is an incredibly intuitive system that allows even a novice to fly through complex environments within minutes. For professional FPV pilots who prefer the precision of manual acrobatic flight, the A1 does support a traditional “Mode 2” stick controller, but the motion controls are so fluid that most owners will likely never switch back.

In a recent development, the marketing for the Antigravity 360 proudly displays “8K Resolution.” In a traditional camera, 8K means every pixel is packed into a 16:9 rectangle. In 360 video, those pixels are spread across a full sphere. When you “reframe” that 8K sphere into a standard flat video, you are looking at a “crop” of the total image.

Sources indicate that the color science is noticeably improved over previous 360 cameras. The A1 features a “Vivid” profile for those who want punchy, social-media-ready colors, and a 10-bit “Log” profile for professional editors who need to match the footage to other cameras in a color-grading suite. The stabilization, powered by Antigravity’s “FlowState” algorithms, is nothing short of miraculous. You can fly in 20mph winds, and the footage remains as steady as if the camera were on a tripod.

The “Antigravity Studio” app allows you to download footage wirelessly (at speeds up to 80MB/s) and reframe your video using your phone’s gyroscope. You simply watch the video and move your phone around to “film” the scene in real-time. The app also features “Auto-Frame,” an AI tool that identifies subjects and automatically generates a cut that keeps them in focus. For a solo creator, this effectively provides a virtual camera crew that never misses a shot.

Recent findings suggest that battery technology remains the bottleneck for all small drones. The A1’s standard Intelligent Flight Battery provides a theoretical 24 minutes of flight. In real-world conditions with moderate wind and constant recording, expect closer to 19 or 20 minutes.

While 20 minutes sounds short, the “work per minute” is much higher than a traditional drone. Because you don’t need to re-fly a path to get different angles, a single 20-minute flight can yield the same amount of usable footage as three flights with a Mavic. For those who need more time, the “Pro Battery” (which pushes the weight over 250g) offers a staggering 39 minutes of flight time, though it does compromise the drone’s agility slightly.

In a recent development, in terms of flight dynamics, the A1 is a “cinewhoop” style flyer. It is stable and predictable rather than aggressive and twitchy. It has a top speed of roughly 36 mph, which is plenty for following bikes or cars, but it won’t keep up with a professional racing drone. The “Turtle Mode” is a life-saver; if you crash and end up upside down, the drone can flip itself over using its propellers, allowing you to take off again without a “walk of shame” to recover the aircraft.

The Antigravity 360 is a niche product that is rapidly becoming mainstream.

It has been revealed that the Antigravity 360 (A1) is the most exciting drone I have tested. By removing the need for a gimbal and the stress of manual framing, it allows the pilot to focus on the one thing that truly matters: the story they are trying to tell.

While the image quality isn’t quite at the level of a high-end cinema drone, and the lenses are admittedly delicate, these are small prices to pay for the creative liberation the A1 provides. It bridges the gap between traditional cinematography and the immersive world of VR.

If you are a creator who is tired of the same old “drone shots” and want to push the boundaries of what is possible in the air, the Antigravity 360 is an essential addition to your toolkit.

#86. Tech Report: United Airlines Bans AI Booking Agents, But Who Is It Really Protecting?

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10 min read (1930 words)
AI & Tech 🌐 Liveandletsfly

Tech Report: United Airlines Bans AI Booking Agents, But Who Is It Really Protecting?

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read | Source: Liveandletsfly

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, united Airlines is restricting third-party AI assistants from booking and managing tickets, citing privacy and safety concerns.
  • In a November 11 announcement, United stated it is restricting unauthorized third-party personal AI agents across its digital platforms and through travel agencies and aggregators.
  • The airline warns that sharing credentials with these tools could expose sensitive information or lead to unwanted purchases and account changes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, united Airlines is restricting third-party AI assistants from booking and managing tickets, citing privacy and safety concerns. I think there is a much more compelling commercial explanation: United understands what happens when passengers have an assistant that continually watches fares and captures savings after they book. The airline is getting ahead of that possibility, and I find its attempt to present this as customer protection rather unconvincing.

In a November 11 announcement, United stated it is restricting unauthorized third-party personal AI agents across its digital platforms and through travel agencies and aggregators.

The airline warns that sharing credentials with these tools could expose sensitive information or lead to unwanted purchases and account changes. It also raises regulatory concerns, pointing to the acknowledgment passengers must make concerning hazardous materials during check-in.

Those concerns deserve consideration. But they do not adequately explain why an assistant should be prohibited from making a change that I understand, authorize, and could make myself.

United has added the following to its prohibited ticketing practices:.

“The use of AI Agents to make, modify or service a Ticket, and/or to purchase any service or product.”.

The definition encompasses autonomous and semi-autonomous assistants, including those whose actions a passenger supervises or approves.

Recent findings suggest that we already have tools that monitor airfare and notify us when prices change. I use fare alerts myself. But receiving an alert still leaves me with work to do. I must examine the offer, check the restrictions, and determine whether changing the ticket actually leaves me better off.

Imagine an assistant doing that work continuously, then completing an authorized change whenever the savings justify it based on the parameters I input at the start of the process…something I would happily use.

Consider a hypothetical $800 ticket whose rules allow you to rebook at a lower fare and retain the difference as a future flight credit, with no change fee.

The price drops to $650. Your AI assistant identifies the same flight and fare conditions, completes the permitted change, and secures a $150 credit.

Later, the price drops to $575. It does the calculation again and captures another $75.

You still take the flight you intended to take, but now have $225 available toward future travel.

It has been revealed that that is not a cash refund on a nonrefundable ticket, and the actual opportunity depends on the fare rules. But evaluating those complications is precisely what would make the technology useful. Tell it what you want to preserve and when it may act. Let it calculate whether the lower price represents actual savings.

Sources indicate that airline revenue management benefits from passengers behaving differently. Some book early, some wait, and some keep checking after buying. Many understandably consider the transaction finished once the confirmation email arrives.

An assistant that keeps shopping changes that calculation.

It has been revealed that A brief fare reduction that I would otherwise miss becomes an opportunity and a small saving that would not justify 20 minutes of my time may become worthwhile when software handles the work. Multiply that across millions of reservations and you can understand why an airline might become uncomfortable.

Recent findings suggest that it would put serious pressure on the ability to retain a higher fare from someone whose ticket permits a lower-price exchange. The airline could still set its prices and restrictions, but fewer customers would leave available savings unclaimed merely because they were busy living their lives.

I suspect United understands this very well. This strikes me as a preemptive move to control who can manage a reservation before automated consumer tools become an ordinary part of travel.

These upcoming rules do not suggest that United intends to eliminate every fare alert: the more consequential restriction is preventing the assistant from acting on what it finds.

It has been revealed that I would not hand any application unrestricted control of my MileagePlus account and yes, I do not want software canceling an important trip because it misunderstood an instruction. But those are reasons to establish permissions and accountability.

United’s hazardous-materials example is particularly weak as a justification for prohibiting reservation management. The federal passenger-notification rule requires disclosures and passenger acknowledgment in specified circumstances. Reading that requirement, I do not see why an assistant could not stop and ask the traveler to complete the necessary acknowledgment personally.

According to recent reports, more to the point, checking whether my ticket can be exchanged for a lower fare does not require an assistant to make a declaration about what is inside my suitcase. A responsible system should require approval where needed and limit what software can do. United’s restriction still encompasses an assistant whose actions I supervise and approve.

So no, I do not accept the customer-protection explanation.

Scott Kirby offered a more revealing observation at a Chicago event, according to The Wall Street Journal:.

“To be honest, I don’t want to create another middleman.”.

Sources indicate that I understand why United would prefer to control the customer relationship, but my interests are not identical to United’s. I may want someone working for me, comparing the options and continuing to look after my reservation once United has collected payment.

Industry observers note that I recently examined Kirby’s argument that technology helps make United the best airline in the world. I agree that its app is excellent. Better technology has made my United travel easier. But I also want technology that helps me spend less. An assistant that understands my preferences and captures an eligible fare reduction would be doing exactly that.

Recent findings suggest that united should explain what secure, authorized access would require. Simply blocking an AI assistant carte blanche protects the airline’s control much more clearly than it protects my interests.

United says its restrictions on third-party AI agents protect customers. I think they also–and primarily–protect United from a future in which passengers can monitor and manage reservations far more effectively than they do today.

Just as airlines use complex algorithms to extract the highest fare fro Mme, I want to use technology to help capture savings without having to babysit every reservation.

To me, this looks like a cheap shot dressed up as customer protection. United is entitled to secure its systems, but I am far less sympathetic to using that explanation to block an authorized assistant from helping me obtain a better deal.

The correct perspective, Mattthew. Well articulated.

Recent findings suggest that I use an Ai agent to keep tabs on hotel reservations as they often go down over time. I have saved literally thousands each year doing this. While I tend more towards the self gardening of my flights it is clear that United wants to prevent consumers from fighting back against the airline’s algorithms. Its dirty. Especially given the rise in fares and the destruction of loyalty.

“Someone” can be held accountable when something goes wrong. Technology that tracks and alerts you of fare changes has existed for a while. AI agents are a whole other can of worms.

Forgive me for anthropomorphizing the technology, but my point is that I want to use technology to my advantage just as UA uses technology to its advantage.

According to recent reports, my point is that you use AI agents at your own peril. You may see it as using a tool to fight a major and mighty corporation, but you are doing so by throwing in your lot with an even bigger and more mercurial corporation that is not your friend and certainly won’t take responsibility for the actions of their unaccountable by design agents.

” …I want to use technology to my advantage just as UA uses technology to its advantage.” My thoughts exactly.

Industry observers note that I dont understand the appeal of letting some unaccountable entity have free reign over my financial instruments. Many companies outside of United are (rightly) blocking AI agents from making purchases.

United is also saving their Frontline employees from additional headaches when people using AI to book do not understand why they dont get a carryon or aren’t sitting with their companions.

I’m far more cynical, especially after Kirby’s statement.

Selfishly,I also dont like it evens the playing field for finding deals. If I’m going to spend the time checking on reservations looking for price drops, I should be rewarded for the effort. The number of discounted tickets on a given flight is finite.

Also, if thousands of AI agents are constantly pricing flights on United’s website, will that mess with the pricing algorithm?

Unilateral technology advantage; we can use it in our revenue systems–but if it’s a mistake we get taksey-backseys it was an error. However if the same concept is applied with our business transacting partner, well that’s just unfair and it might cause issues.

Personally I wouldn’t use an agent for this as I enjoy the thrill of the chase but the general public it gives, as you note, a massive leg up in the value wars. The cat is out of the bag and they won’t be able to regulate it effectively even with their own technology–and they shouldn’t to begin with. They’re trying to keep the public in the 1990s while they race ahead for a profit advantage.

I think you’re reducing the argument to “airline wants to prevent customers from saving $50 on fare drops,” and ignoring the much broader implications of unauthorized redistribution, cost of sale, corporate fare integrity, transactional accountability, etc. etc. etc. Something tells me United cares more about that stuff than they do you letting your lil AI agent monitor pricing.

Sources indicate that it would be easier to just drop the ‘no change fees’ nonsense that allows for partial refunds on already purchased tickets just because of a change in availability. They could then sell it as a benefit of expensive fully flexible fare families without trying to catch their customers out.

No way. I hate change fees. They are junk fees that cost the airline nothing.

They carry a genuine, often substantial, opportunity cost which is part of the reason US airlines are more expensive than their international competitors, virtually all of whom offer genuine choice when it comes to flexibility (as opposed to the the real junk fee which is ASR i.e. ‘pay us extra to seat in the type of seat you’ve already got a ticket for’).

You’re completely correct: United just wants all the benefits of technology as long as it benefits them but prohibits tech that helps passengers not get hosed by United. I can’t really say I’m in the least surprised that Kirby is doing this since he’s been very clear that he considers anything that empowers any entity in any way that might be detrimental to him personally or to United to be anathema.
