📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Starlink satellite internet service is now available on more than half of United Airlines’ daily flights, the carrier revealed Thursday.

The airline noted it accelerated Starlink installations ahead of the Thanksgiving travel period. It expects to fly an average of 500,000 people per day between Nov. 19 and Dec. 1.

Customers can use United’s Starlink Wi-Fi tracker to check whether their upcoming flight is equipped with the service up to three days before their departure.

United selected Starlink as its onboard wireless internet provider in 2024. It first installed the technology on its regional jets and is now working on its long-haul widebody fleet.

Starlink Wi-Fi is free for MileagePlus members.

Sources indicate that united expects to have Starlink on nearly 64% of daily flights by the end of the year. Installations should be complete by the end of 2027, officials said.

#62. How a Trip to India Helped Me Find Peace With a Life-Changing Diagnosis

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8 min read (1523 words)
General 🌐 Cntraveler

How a Trip to India Helped Me Find Peace With a Life-Changing Diagnosis

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read | Source: Cntraveler

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that after spending nearly 25 years away, Tina Aswani-Omprakash, 43, finally traveled back to India, confronting long-held fears about traveling with Crohn’s disease.
  • In a recent development, the tuk-tuk ride up the Chamundi Hills near Mysuru, India, took about half an hour.
  • I could feel the air on my face, and I remember thinking, I can’t believe it, but I’m really doing this.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that after spending nearly 25 years away, Tina Aswani-Omprakash, 43, finally traveled back to India, confronting long-held fears about traveling with Crohn’s disease. Along the way she reconnected with her roots, her family, and the food she had spent years afraid to eat. Following more than 20 surgeries and years of debilitating illness, going on the trip was a hard-won milestone for Aswani-Omprakash, made possible through careful preparation and her doctors’ support. Involving everything from exploring historic palaces and temples to meeting some relatives for the first time, the experience reminded her how travel can help us feel connected to culture and live life to the fullest. Here is Aswani-Omprakash’s story, as told to health writer Katie Camero.

In a recent development, the tuk-tuk ride up the Chamundi Hills near Mysuru, India, took about half an hour. My husband, brother-in-law, and some of my colleagues were split between two rickshaws, winding our way up a massive hill toward the Chamundeshwari Temple. I used to love taking tuk-tuks as a kid, but at age 41 I found that the ride felt like so much more than a fun adventure.

I could feel the air on my face, and I remember thinking, I can’t believe it, but I’m really doing this. After over 20 surgeries and some near-death experiences, I had somehow worked up the courage to travel and live my life again.

Gopuram of Sri Chamundeshwari Temple, Chamundi Hill, Mysore, Karnataka, South India.

In a recent development, since childhood I’ve experienced a lot of what doctors call extraintestinal manifestations, which are symptoms that occur when an inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) affects parts of the body outside the gut. I dealt with issues like severe joint pain and eye issues alongside constipation and GERD, but at the time doctors didn’t think to refer me to a gastroenterologist. The discomfort and unpredictability of my condition meant I was always scared to travel, even if it was just a road trip.

Industry observers note that the last time I visited my family in India was in 2000 at age 16. We took a day trip from New Delhi to the Taj Mahal and ended up eating street food because we were starving. We all got sick, but I fared so much worse than the others and lost about 20 pounds in the weeks that followed because I was so ill. I eventually was diagnosed with IBD—specifically, ulcerative colitis—in 2006. (Although later I learned I actually had a different type of IBD.) Nearly two years later, my husband, who was my boyfriend at the time, took me to Mexico and we both came down with traveler’s diarrhea after eating some sliced fruit. He threw it all up and recovered just fine, but it took me months to get better.

What followed was a lot of pain, shame, and silence. I worked on Wall Street at the time as a financial-services compliance officer, and it was very tough to figure out the diagnosis, accept it, and try to get on medication while navigating such a stressful career. I was on disability for many years before I eventually had to stop working. I didn’t know what to do with my life because I truly thought this disease and the complications associated with it would kill me.

Sources indicate that over two years, my condition went from mild to severe. During this time I experienced severe bleeding, weight loss, and other debilitating symptoms. I finally had my colon removed on July 4, 2008—which I often call my very own Independence Day. However, complications from this operation, as well as my IBD itself, required me to have dozens of additional operations including one to create a permanent ileostomy in 2011. It was through this process that I learned I actually have Crohn’s disease, another type of IBD.

Sources indicate that it wasn’t until late 2024 that my doctors finally gave me the green light to travel to India—and I was terrified. The extra-long flight plus cuisines that include many trigger foods for my condition created a hurdle I worried was impossible to overcome. Although I had taken a few trips around the U.S. and Europe since my diagnosis, I had not conquered my fears of traveling back to India and enjoying the foods my family and I love without getting sick.

After all this time, I thought I couldn’t do this because of my Crohn’s disease. Yet there I was almost 25 years later. I did it—albeit with lots of preparation.

Recent findings suggest that my doctors did an intestinal ultrasound and other tests to make sure nothing was brewing in my gut, and they gave me antibiotics, steroids, and probiotics in case I had a flare-up or bad case of traveler’s diarrhea. My husband and I also booked a hotel, which our relatives didn’t love, but it gave me easy access to filtered water (tap water could have been contaminated with harmful bacteria that could make me really sick) and a private bathroom in case I needed to make frequent trips overnight, along with other perks that kept us feeling safe and comfortable. I stayed clear of street vendors and only ate hot foods to reduce my chances of getting ill.

Even with those restrictions I enjoyed delicious, authentic food. In Mysuru, there’s a restaurant called MTR that offers South Indian cuisine like dosas, which I love. Though the lentil soup they come with can be a little spicy (a common IBD trigger), you can ask for a plain dosa with potatoes inside, which actually works pretty well for people with IBD. It’s a good way for us to enjoy the local cuisine while avoiding a flare-up.

Though it may seem like a lot of work, it honestly felt like such a huge accomplishment to go back to where my family is from and connect with my culture and relatives, some of whom I’d never met before, without getting sick.

However, it took a lot to get to that point. I faced many cultural challenges, not just during my journey to a diagnosis but also to starting treatment. My family survived the 1947 partition of India and Pakistan—my relatives were displaced from Pakistan and became refugees in India. As a result my family lost their trust in the West, and they certainly did not trust Western medicine. My condition got more severe than it needed to because my family was so against medicine or surgery. Marriageability and how others will perceive the family is also something my community worries about a lot. So I had to consider how my diagnosis would impact my sibling’s ability to find partners.

I felt a lot of fear as well because my dad died when I was 8 years old from Crohn’s disease that turned into colorectal cancer. Despite having this family history, I had to do a ton of self-advocacy to finally get the colonoscopy that started to give me much-needed answers and treatment options.

It has been revealed that through all of this I’ve learned that fear is just a mindset and we can accomplish whatever we want if we believe in ourselves. It also really takes a certain mindset to travel such a long distance and eat foods you haven’t been able to eat in so many years without feeling completely terrified you’re going to get sick.

It has been revealed that because of the stigmas I faced in my own journey with IBD, I co-founded, alongside other patient advocates and clinicians, the Strategic Alliance for Intercultural Advocacy in GI, a nonprofit that offers culturally sensitive resources for patients with GI conditions, caregivers, and health care providers to improve treatment and access to care. Many patients I speak with ask why I push past my comfort zone through my travels. My answer is simple: It makes me feel alive. With everything I went through in my 20s and 30s with this disease, I felt like I wasn’t really living. But when you go through so much disability, all you want to do is feel alive again.

It has been revealed that of course, trips like these aren’t feasible for everyone with inflammatory bowel disease. But if you start slowly, you might just surprise yourself. Growing with and owning your chronic illness is a process, and travel has helped me with that immeasurably.

#61. New Credit Card Sets Annual Fee Dynamically, Based On Benefit Usage

New Credit Card Sets Annual Fee Dynamically, Based On Benefit Usage

📅 02 Apr 2025 | ⏱️ 3 min read | Source: Godsavethepoints

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, among savvy Redditors and credit card blogs, there’s a common thread with many recent credit card changes.
  • Since many people simply won’t use all the benefits and partner offers being baked into the card, people increasingly feel like the annual fee rises are getting too steep.
  • In a recent development, signed up for a card named after a precious or semi precious metal and shocked by the $450-$695 fee?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, among savvy Redditors and credit card blogs, there’s a common thread with many recent credit card changes. “It feels like a coupon book” is often the consumer reaction, particularly as annual fees rise as justification for an increasing number of partner offer benefits, which if consumed in entirety could lead to more value.

Since many people simply won’t use all the benefits and partner offers being baked into the card, people increasingly feel like the annual fee rises are getting too steep. In a bold move, a latest card launched today which offers a flexible annual fee, based only on the benefits you actually use.

In a recent development, signed up for a card named after a precious or semi precious metal and shocked by the $450-$695 fee? You’re not alone.

To get your money back from such a fee, you’d need to take advantage of regular lounge access at airports, utilize your TSA PreCheck/Global Entry credit, maximize every monthly dining or entertainment credit and sign up for every other fee credit, which often requires a purchase.

To quell this matter, the newly introduced card is effectively a build your own card, card.

Despite the innovation, the card draws on the historical concept of the coupon book, where you only pay for the offers you tear out and redeem. The annual fee starts at zero, but as you actually redeem the cards benefits, you get billed accordingly. Your fee can be zero, or as high as $10,000 per year.

Done right, you can end up paying $650 in annual fees for about $800 worth of stuff, some of which you wanted and most of which, about $700 worth, you didn’t really want or need, but felt compelled to get, just because it’s there.

This model allows you to really dive into the classic coupon book, feeling like you’re really tearing offers out of the page, and simply leaving the ones you’re not using in the book. You’re only paying for the ones you rip out, but when there’s so many offers to choose from, the book just feels so compelling.

Obviously, it’s April 1st and no such card is coming to the market (yet, lol), but hopefully this light hearted amusement has been a helpful exercise in framing the true value you’re really extracting from your premium credit card, or conversely, the lack thereof.

Industry observers note that consider the things you’d actually purchase without the “offer” prompt and if that number still adds up to be more than the annual fee, you’re doing it right. If it doesn’t….

#60. Global Airlines Liquidating: The Senseless A380 Dream Finally Dies

Global Airlines Liquidating: The Senseless A380 Dream Finally Dies

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read | Source: Onemileatatime

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the past few years, I’ve extensively covered Global Airlines, the strange “airline startup” that had a single Airbus A380, with which it wanted to bring back the “golden age” of travel.
  • Public records in the UK show that Global Airlines has finally been given winding up orders, which is the equivalent of liquidation.
  • In a recent development, this means that a government officer from the Insolvency Service will now become the liquidator, and take control of the organization, investigate its affairs and the conduct of directors, and collect whatever assets still exist for creditors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the past few years, I’ve extensively covered Global Airlines, the strange “airline startup” that had a single Airbus A380, with which it wanted to bring back the “golden age” of travel. The carrier’s A380 has been parked since the spring of 2025, and just several months ago, I covered how the company faced several winding up petitions. Well, there’s now an upgrade, which seems long overdue….

Public records in the UK show that Global Airlines has finally been given winding up orders, which is the equivalent of liquidation. This is in response to a petition that was filed on May 29, 2026, and a court approved that order on November 4, 2026. This has only been added to public records today, as there seems to be a one week period between when these decisions are made, and when they’re published for the public.

In a recent development, this means that a government officer from the Insolvency Service will now become the liquidator, and take control of the organization, investigate its affairs and the conduct of directors, and collect whatever assets still exist for creditors. This means that the directors no longer have control of the company.

What’s amazing about this entire story is that in the spring of 2025, the manufacturer actually operated two roundtrip flights to New York out of Europe, for reasons that most of us couldn’t really make sense of. For that matter, this was part of a wet lease agreement with Portuguese charter company Hi-Fly, given that Global Airlines lacked its own operating certificate.

James Asquith, founder of Global Airlines, gate crashes travel guru Simon Calder's interview with Mike Graham.@james_asquith: "Did you get a cupcake?"@Iromg | @SimonCalder pic.twitter.com/etMVj1TcPu.

It has been revealed that shortly after the A380 operated those flights, it entered long term storage, as it needed to undergo heavy maintenance, which costs millions of dollars. The company’s founder, James Asquith, had insisted that the reason the plane was parked for so long was due to delays with being able to get heavy maintenance.

Just months ago, Asquith suggested that the airline would be flying to the Maldives before the end of 2026, despite no progress having been made on the heavy maintenance front.

A post shared by Robyn Asquith (@robynasquith).

Obviously on the surface, the whole Global Airlines thing sounds a bit odd. But let me simply say that the public knows only a tiny fraction of what was really going on here. That’s true both in terms of what Asquith was showing investors to get them onboard with the concept, and also what he claimed the goals for the company were.

My skepticism with this concept wasn’t because I don’t like to see other people succeed, or because I’m against innovation, or anything like that. Instead, it’s because things aren’t always what they seem, and when you’re raising millions of dollars of other people’s money and selling them a dream, there has to be some chance of that actually becoming a reality.

Sources indicate that keep in mind that in 2025, Asquith appeared on The Times’ 40 richest people under 40 list, which claimed he had a net worth of £183 million, making him richer than Adele. Right.

It has been revealed that I’d encourage those who just went along with Asquith to be a little introspective here. For example, when you have publications like SimpleFlying that publish things about Global Airlines without even an ounce of skepticism, and then you have people like Captain Chris who latch on to people like Asquith as if they’re Richard Branson (which he literally compared him to, while pointing out that he was proving the doubters wrong), that’s a problem.

A post shared by Captain Chris | Aviation Life (@captainchris).

It has been revealed that many people lost many millions of dollars on this venture. Now, I’d also encourage them to perhaps be a bit more careful next time. And if you just want to make a donation to someone with no expectation of any return, I’m also happy to wire you my bank account details. 😉.

Sources indicate that it’s the end of the road (or runway) for Global Airlines, as the A380 “airline” has had its winding up petition approved, meaning the company will now be liquidated. It was only a matter of time before this was going to happen, so I don’t think anyone will be surprised. Hopefully one day the entire story can come to light….

American Airlines is planning to add more flights from Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), as part of a “gradual build” at its West Coast hub.

The Fort Worth-based carrier stated it's about to add more LAX service to its schedule, with a focus on places executives describe as “vital markets.”.

It’s not clear whether that means entirely fresh routes or more frequent service on existing ones.

But either way, it comes after a long stretch where American seemed to focus far more of its attention on other parts of the country.

After the pandemic, the airline doubled down on its Sun Belt hubs, fortifying its strongholds in Dallas, Charlotte and Miami.

More recently, American reignited a longstanding Chicago turf war with United Airlines when it rapidly reinstated flying at O’Hare International Airport (ORD).

It looks like LAX will be its next project.

“We’re going to grow," American chief commercial officer Nat Pieper said, speaking this week at an industry conference. "We’re going to tailor a schedule to the local market.".

American has a smaller presence today in Southern California than it did several years ago.

This year, the carrier will operate about 32% fewer flights than it did in 2019, according to data from aviation analytics firm Cirium.

That’s a significant drop-off at LAX, which is one of the nation’s most competitive airports — and the only where each of the “substantial three” legacy carriers operates a hub.

According to recent reports, by contrast, top L.A. rival Delta Air Lines has solidified its place as the airport’s top carrier, and plans operate its largest-ever schedule there next year.

United Airlines has also signaled it has future growth aspirations at LAX.

Speaking earlier this year, United’s top network planner, Patrick Quayle, lamented the fact that the airport is United’s only hub where there’s another airline with a larger presence.

“I don’t like being No. 2,” Quayle noted during a tech giant event at LAX in March. “And so I will, today, put Delta on notice here in L.A. — we will be No. 1, as well.”'.

Pieper said the carrier needs to start by catering more to local Los Angeles customers — not just using the airport as a hub to route connecting traffic.

Doing that, he acknowledged, will likely require AA to offer a longer list of unique destinations.

Today, for instance, the carrier only serves four long-haul cities from LAX: London, Tokyo, Sydney and Auckland.

“People don’t only want to fly domestically. They want to go to Latin America. They want to go to Europe. They want to go to Asia,” Pieper said on stage this week at the Skift Aviation Forum in New York. “We need to be able to serve that with our own airplanes.”.

Recent findings suggest that united is clearly following that formula. The carrier already serves more than a half-dozen transpacific destinations from Southern California — and will expand next year with a new route to Osaka.

Industry observers note that delta, for its part, is also pointing to LAX as a linchpin of its Pacific growth aspirations, having launched nonstops to Hong Kong and Melbourne within the past year. New flights to Manila will begin in 2027.

Delta’s Los Angeles growth is also thanks, in part, to massive infrastructure investments the carrier has made at the hub which, among other things, is the only airport that's home to two Delta One Lounges.

American’s LAX digs, meanwhile, are still a construction zone.

The carrier had to consolidate its presence at the airport last year to make way for a rebuild of the airport's Terminal 5.

American will grow at a "gradual" pace, Pieper said, until its LAX facilities are "ready to roll." That's expected to happen in late 2028, at which point the carrier will have access to 30 gates.

“Our facility will be as good as anybody’s,” he mentioned.

That, along with more flights — plus connectivity to American's Pacific partners like Qantas and Japan Airlines— have the airline more bullish about its hub that's grabbed far fewer headlines in recent years.

“You combine all those things together,” Pieper added, “I think we’re going to have a compelling offering there.”.

A Wonderfully Relaxing “Afternoon Matinée” In SAS A330 Business Class

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our SAS A330-300 Business Class flight from Copenhagen to Chicago could not have been better and it really was one of the most relaxing flights I’ve had in a long time, during which I enjoyed great food and watched two excellent movies when I could not sleep.

Unless I’m flying on a plane with Starlink, I assume that the internet is not going to work onboard (especially on SAS). If it does, it is a pleasant surprise. If not, in most cases I will have already completed essential tasks so that I’m not spending my flight dreading unfinished work.

We flew home on Sunday afternoon, also a day off for me, and I decided that I’d just relax and watch some movies during the flight if I could not sleep between meals.

Lunch, by the way, was delicious. I pre-ordered “ASC” salmon with tomato vinaigrette, summer cabbage with brown butter, Jerusalem artichoke soufflé, and chive oil while Heidi pre-ordered beef with osso buco sauce, polenta cake, butter-and-thyme carrot, grilled artichoke and gremolata. We shared. Both dishes were perfect.

The appetizer and dessert were also excellent, as was the coffee:.

I find the catering consistently excellent on SAS.

It has been revealed that I did try to sleep, but could not, but that turned out to be a blessing in disguise on this flight. First I watched a Japanese movie called A Pale View of Hills, which I found riveting and very well-done. It trace the story of Etsuko and has a beautiful twist that left me profoundly moved. Highly recommended.

Meanwhile, Heidi was watching a German movie called Sound of Falling, a psychological drama spanning a century at a farmhouse in rural Germany. I then watched that while she watched the Japanese move. Wow, also excellent. Riveting and thought-provoking.

We don’t have a TV at home and I do not watch movies or anything at all unless I’m on a plane, but watching movies like this makes me think that I may be missing out…both were so well done and absolutely worth the time. I honestly could not stop thinking about either one for a couple days.

Before a landing, a delicious open-face sandwich was served with eggs and shrimp.

The flight crew was excellent and the kids were again very well-behaved, so I really don’t think it could have been a better flight. SAS does not have a cutting edge business class seat, but between my six hours of sleep on the way to Copenhagen and my restful flight on the way back, I was reminded again how much I love fly SAS Business Class and hope that I can find a way to replenish my EuroBonus account once we spend down the rest of the two million points.

I’m not sure whether I will offer a full review of this flight…I took a lot more pictures, but I’ve reviewed this product recently and little has changed. Bottom line: I do strongly recommend SAS for intercontinental travel.

#55. Alaska Airlines Aims To Connect Tokyo From Anchorage, But Can Only Do It With 1 Boeing 737

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8 min read (1549 words)
General 🌐 Simpleflying

Alaska Airlines Aims To Connect Tokyo From Anchorage, But Can Only Do It With 1 Boeing 737

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read | Source: Simpleflying

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Alaska Airlines will launch its first nonstop service between Ted Stevens Anchorage International Airport (ANC) and Tokyo Narita Airport (NRT) in 2027, opening a direct link between the largest city in Alaska and one of Asia’s most crucial aviation gateways.
  • Industry observers note that the headline’s reference to one Boeing 737 is about aircraft capability, not a proposal to dedicate only one physical airframe to the route.
  • In a recent development, alaska announced it will begin the route on May 13, 2027, with daily flights through September 7.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alaska Airlines will launch its first nonstop service between Ted Stevens Anchorage International Airport (ANC) and Tokyo Narita Airport (NRT) in 2027, opening a direct link between the largest city in Alaska and one of Asia’s most crucial aviation gateways. The route will be unusual not only because the cities have never had scheduled nonstop service on Alaska, but because the airline intends to operate it with a single-aisle aircraft. A Boeing 737 MAX 8 will cover the transpacific journey, which is scheduled to take as long as eight hours and 15 minutes westbound.

Industry observers note that the headline’s reference to one Boeing 737 is about aircraft capability, not a proposal to dedicate only one physical airframe to the route. Alaska’s MAX 8 is the only 737 variant in its fleet with sufficient range for the mission. The larger MAX 10, which the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) certified in October 2026 and which Alaska expects to begin receiving in the second quarter of 2027, cannot operate the route with the same capability.

In a recent development, alaska announced it will begin the route on May 13, 2027, with daily flights through September 7. The airline intends to resume service in January 2028 at three flights per week, extending the link beyond the initial summer season. AeroRoutes reports that flight AS21 is scheduled to depart Anchorage at 2:10 PM and arrive at Tokyo Narita at 3:25 PM the following day. The return, AS22, leaves Narita at 9:45 PM and reaches Anchorage at noon on the same calendar day. All times are local, and the date change reflects the route’s crossing of the International Date Line. The seasonal pattern also leaves a gap between the end of the summer schedule in September and the planned winter restart in January.

The flight’s duration may appear surprising for a 737, but Anchorage and Tokyo are geographically closer than their positions on a conventional map suggest. The airports are separated by approximately 2,980 nautical miles (5,519 km). Both cities sit at relatively high latitudes, shortening the trans-Pacific distance compared with routes linking Tokyo to major US cities farther south. The westbound schedule of up to eight hours and 15 minutes is only marginally longer than Alaska’s Anchorage–New York-JFK route, despite crossing the North Pacific. The new service is not the longest route Alaska has flown with the MAX 8 by distance; its seasonal Seattle–Reykjavík service covers a greater distance.

Sources indicate that alaska has explicitly identified the 737 MAX 8 as the only aircraft in its 737 fleet capable of operating Anchorage–Tokyo. The airline claims the MAX 8 has greater range than the MAX 10, even though the latter is the larger member of the family. A longer fuselage and higher passenger capacity can increase weight, while fuel capacity, aerodynamic performance, and maximum takeoff weight influence how far an aircraft can fly.

Alaska lists the MAX 8 with a range of approximately 3,500 nautical miles (6,482 km). The route’s published distance sits relatively close to that headline figure, which helps explain why the MAX 8 is selected rather than a higher-capacity aircraft. Airlines calculate actual dispatch capability using expected winds, temperature, required reserves, alternate-airport requirements, and the payload being carried. That level of nuance and margin is also likely why Alaska chose not to use the MAX 9, even though its maximum range technically covers the ANC-NRT route distance.

The MAX 10’s arrival will therefore not make the MAX 8 redundant on Alaska’s longest narrowbody missions. The FAA issued the MAX 10’s amended type certificate on October 20, 2026, clearing the aircraft for delivery after a prolonged certification process. Alaska expects its first examples from the second quarter of 2027, but their role will be shaped by different network requirements.

Late night Seattle departures connect to early morning arrivals in Guadalajara three times weekly aboard 737-800.

The aircraft assigned to the route is configured with 161 seats, including 16 in First Class and 145 across the rest of the cabin. This is Alaska’s standard domestic-style MAX 8 layout, not a dedicated international configuration. First Class passengers will receive recliner seats, not lie-flat beds, and the aircraft does not offer individual seatback entertainment screens.

According to recent reports, alaska is adding service elements intended to make the journey more comfortable. Its route announcement describes multi-course dining in First Class, complimentary meals in Main Cabin and Premium Class, and Filson-branded bedding and amenity kits for First Class passengers. The airline is also expanding connectivity across its MAX 8 fleet through Starlink installations, although its announcement states free Wi-Fi is available on select flights as the rollout continues.

Recent findings suggest that an eight-hour flight places more emphasis on personal space, sleep, and entertainment than a typical domestic sector. Travelers choosing First Class will have a larger recliner and upgraded service, but not a lie-flat product. The introductory round-trip fare was confirmed from $999 for travel between May 13 and June 7, 2027, subject to availability and the original booking deadline.

It has been revealed that aircraft range alone does not determine whether a nonstop flight can operate safely. Because the 737 MAX 8 has two engines, Anchorage–Tokyo must comply with extended-range twin-engine operational requirements, commonly known as ETOPS. These rules require airlines to proposal routes so that an aircraft remains within its approved diversion time of suitable alternate airports. Dispatchers must identify alternates and confirm that weather forecasts and runway conditions meet the applicable operating standards for the period in which the aircraft might need to land.

It has been revealed that the North Pacific presents particular planning challenges. There are fewer major airports than on many transatlantic corridors, and weather at remote airfields can change rapidly. Alaska and the Aleutian Islands provide potential diversion options along parts of the route, while airports in Japan offer alternatives closer to the destination. However, an airport is not automatically usable simply because it appears geographically convenient. Its runway, rescue and firefighting services, operating hours, facilities, and forecast conditions must satisfy the airline’s requirements.

Industry observers note that these constraints can affect how much payload the aircraft carries. Fuel reserves and the ability to reach an alternate must be protected, while stronger-than-expected headwinds can increase fuel burn and reduce the weight available for passengers, baggage, and cargo. Under 14 CFR 121.624, an operator must list enough ETOPS alternate airports within the approved diversion time and ensure they meet weather and field-condition requirements.

Alaska Airlines is launching two seven-hour Honolulu routes as its growing Boeing 737 MAX fleet opens new opportunities.

The Tokyo route is part of a broader expansion at Anchorage. Alaska has also declared seasonal nonstop flights to Austin, Dallas-Fort Worth, and Nashville, creating four upcoming routes from the city in 2027. Those domestic services will operate weekly on Saturdays during the summer, while Tokyo will have a much more substantial schedule.

It has been revealed that the route also extends Alaska’s international ambitions beyond Seattle. The airline has added London, Rome, and Reykjavík from its Pacific Northwest hub with the Boeing 787, alongside existing services to Asia. Its Seattle expansion, outlined in an airline announcement, relies on a combination of widebody aircraft, narrowbody MAX 8 services, and partnerships that provide onward connections. Anchorage–Tokyo applies the narrowbody model differently: rather than linking Seattle to a European destination, it uses Alaska’s northern location to establish a direct trans-Pacific connection.

In a recent development, the airline will need to build demand on both sides of the route. Japanese visitors can use Anchorage as a gateway to Alaska’s national parks, wildlife, and cruise ports, while travelers from Alaska gain direct access to Tokyo and connections beyond Narita. Narita offers connections across Japan and to other Asian destinations, although the usefulness of those connections will depend on partner schedules and minimum connection times. The winter reduction to three weekly flights suggests Alaska expects demand to vary by season.

Anchorage–Tokyo is a carefully targeted use of the 737 MAX 8 rather than evidence that every narrowbody can serve long-haul markets without compromise. The aircraft’s range makes the route possible, but payload limits, ETOPS planning, and the passenger experience will determine whether the schedule is sustainable. It is the only 737 in Alaska’s fleet that can perform the mission with the proper safety margins.

Recent findings suggest that if the route attracts enough year-round demand, Anchorage could become more than a seasonal spoke in Alaska’s (and Seattle's) network. It may provide a platform for additional trans-Pacific flying, particularly to destinations that cannot yet support widebody frequencies. Future aircraft deliveries and changes in the airline’s fleet could broaden those options, but the immediate test is whether a 161-seat aircraft can reliably connect Alaska and Japan across changing seasonal conditions. The route’s success will depend less on the headline flight time than on consistent performance, useful onward connections, and passenger demand in both directions. A strong first season could also give Alaska evidence for testing other long-range narrowbody markets from Anchorage, while weak winter bookings would reinforce the value of keeping such routes seasonal rather than forcing year-round capacity.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, yesterday, a Hi-Fly charter airplane took off from Glasgow bound for New York, with Hi-Fly crews and pilots. If you read the papers, it was purportedly ‘Global Airlines’ maiden flight, even though there’s no regularly scheduled service, the pilots and crew weren’t theirs, they couldn’t legally sell airline tickets on their own website and they don’t have a license to operate.

In 2025, crazy things are par for the course, so that didn’t stop all sorts of promising headlines of a revolution in the skies. This is the airline that promised stunning innovation and joy in the air, and the press gave Global Airlines an early gift, by comparing the story to Richard Branson and Virgin Atlantic. That’s just insane, as you’ll soon read.

In reality, anyone can charter a plane and have Hi-Fly operate it, and anyone foolish enough can pay extra for a custom paint job with their logo, or more financially insane — buy a scrapyard A380 and be on the hook for its maintenance, while paying a third party to fly it.

Sources indicate that the whole ‘Global’ pitch was that people love the Airbus A380, hate all the current global airline experiences ( really?) and airline services — and a revolution in the skies, can happen again. It sounded exciting. We all like to dream. Global’s first flight would be the testament to what air travel can be and something passengers love. So, how’d they do?

When Virgin Atlantic launched in 1984, the airline industry had been in a massively “beige” management consultant style, joy killer phase for a decade.

Sources indicate that the fun “golden era” aircraft spaces and frills of the 60’s had largely been stripped out and bus travel comparisons were totally fair. Richard Branson’s light hearted approach to service and differentiated selling could shift dollars and votes — and measurably did.

Sources indicate that let me be very clear: that simplicity in differentiation is no longer the case. You cannot shift wallets and put butts in seats just by saying you have a cool airplane alone, or a bar on board (particularly when it’s just a beverage cart that indicates pub).

From leading (actually real) global airlines, passengers expect, at minimum, the following….

When “Global”, and by Global I really do legally, technically mean Hi-Fly the jet charter company which actually flew the scrapyard plane that “Global” bought, they did NOT have….

It has been revealed that travel blogger Noel Phillips shared some of the trip with his following. The following screen grabs are…. cute?

According to recent reports, the truth is, Virgin Atlantic didn’t have nearly as gargantuan of a task in the 80’s as any airline coming to market does today. In the 80’s many airlines were stuck, did lack innovation and had a pool of largely uninspired talent, with no experience outside of the airline vertical. There also wasn’t this whole technology thing, as standard expectation.

That’s all so far from the case these days and most that are specialized in the airline world are wickedly sharp. Most new people I know at airlines now also come from major tech companies, other travel verticals or impactful innovation firms.

Airlines are getting pretty good at this ole’ air travel thing.

A differentiated approach to smiles on board and a little bit of extra focus on fun, food and drinks could really shift minds and mentalities in the 1980’s, but now you gotta back it up, baby.

Everyone likes to feel special and Virgin, forever, has made people feel special at a time without tech. I’d argue Virgin has taught Delta a lot about that, and it’s a contributing factor to Delta’s rise as a premium airline. It didn’t happen overnight, and what looks easy never is.

Getting people to fly with you is now about safety, reliability, excellence in mobile technology, schedule and personalization. Then fine, we can care about which champagne; or caterer or lounge style or airport, and which celebs like it. Yes, these legacy airlines can appear stuffy at times, but my god, can you not marvel at the technology revolution making air travel journeys excellent?

On real airlines, before I even arrive at the airport, I can use the NFC chip in my passport pressed against my phone to validate my document and bypass human interaction. I board a United, or any serious airline flight nowadays and see a notification that my bag is loaded onto a cart to be loaded on the plane, then again when it’s loaded onto the plane!

I hit the wifi and I’m connected sitting at the gate. If for some reason the flight is at all delayed, or connection in jeopardy, I can instantly rebook onto any other service at no charge, without talking to a soul, with just a tap on the app.

Recent findings suggest that their seag back screens have blockbuster movies, boxsets and everything else you could want for a one hour, or 15 hour journey. It’s all just standard now, not innovative.

The app navigates me through the airport and even tells me when my zone is boarding. AKA – stand the “f” back. The food is at least solid, the beverages are getting better because of their scale (buying power) and there are fewer poor customer service interactions because of how tech forward and seamless journeys are.

According to recent reports, all the great, big airlines do this. This is like… baseline for a real player.

Tell me, or ask the Global Airlines CEO, James Asquith, where in the roadmap all of these essentials are? I want to make it clear that their priority for the last three years was a Soho House press conference about serving champagne in economy, maybe, “if they could get the economics right” rather than any of these basic things.

And in the end, they didn’t even deliver on the silly things they prioritized. The first Global flight wasn’t a remotely differentiated take on economy, business or first, as promised. It was 12 year old seats from another lackluster airline, without real refurb and even the long haul dignity of any seat back entertainment, which that airline which scrapped the plane offered.

If Richard Branson was at the helm, they never would’ve let that flight take off. Making a splash means at least doing one thing differently, right? An airline promising total innovation, A380 experience and differentiation cannot launch a flight which does not even meet the basic standards of budget carriers like Norse. You just can’t take off. You innovative something!

Industry observers note that let’s not forget that when Richard Branson formed Virgin Atlantic, he’d already founded a notable brand and number of businesses in the UK, was quite famous, and filed records and tech giant books in a place where they are scrutinized. He was “real”, even if some was bluster. The public could and did use his businesses.

James Asquith’s only claim to fame, other than from the Instagram account he bought followers for, to fake fame — yes, factually — is that he was the “CEO” of Holiday Swap. Omg, so massive time!

Recent findings suggest that the business purports to be a home swap firm, though there are no financial records of any legal merit in the West, and despite my damndest multi-year attempts, no record of actual customers. Simple use of Similar Web or review sites will help your own conclusions. You can read old blog posts for more musings. The rumors of what laundered through are scary. Maybe a real journalist can find out for us?

I actually think it’s dangerous to the public to compare these two people.

Sources indicate that I’ve had the good fortune of meeting Richard Branson many times throughout the years and he’s always been wildly impressive. Wickedly sharp, analytical, funny and personable. It’s easy to put in a good shift for PR purposes, but I’ve observed levels of deep dive knowledge that no setup encounter can protect for — and genuine interest too. He cares about his people and he worries about the details.

I also have many people in my personal life connected to the Virgin Atlantic founder and I know of nothing but admiration and respect for the man, his company ethos and family. Business in the front, party in the back.

Industry observers note that my only encounter with James Asquith was when he was fuming that he wasn’t invited on an airlines press trip, slid into my Instagram DM’s wanting me to blast them – and for us to be best buds as we roast a major (actual) global airline. That airline later confidentially told me he was banned from flying, due to his antics. I politely declined and he unfollowed me. It was soooo cool.

I guess if you can’t fly other airlines, you start your own?

So yeah, if you ever feel like putting your life in the hands of an airline without functioning entertainment screens, or WiFi, or regularly scheduled service, or new seats, or a mobile app, or an actual license to fly planes, definitely fly with Global. Oh, and no viable loyalty program either. Forget about earning points from daily spending and turning them into upgrades.

Those other “boring” airlines with all the bells and whistles above are clearly not ready to make travel great, with a latest golden age, again.

It has been revealed that gilbert Ott is an ever curious traveler and one of the world's leading travel experts. His adventures take him all over the globe, often spanning over 200,000 miles a year and his travel exploits are regularly... More by Gilbert Ott.

Industry observers note that his intrusion and snide comment ab0ut Simon Calder was entirely unnecessary. I have little respect for Asquith as it is, he doesn’t seem to actually “do” anything other than post Insta’s of slamming Champagne, and buying an Instagram account for the new venture is downright deceptive. Prove me wrong, I’m all for new carriers, but part of me wants it to fail just because of the insufferable “CEO”.

‘Global Airlines’ reminds me of the line from ‘The Producers’: “Under the right circumstances, a [person] could make more money with a flop than he could with a hit.”.

Sources indicate that this is why many say “hire for personality and train for skill.” James Asquith has failed this test with his attitude and stands little chance of building a culture within his firm that can grow to compete with the likes of Virgin. I was always concerned that this airline was launching without any unique selling points at all. Now to read that what little was brought in from China Southern does not even work: it’s for me very sad to read. Substantial funding was needed to get this far and there seems to have been very little planning around the customer experience. I raised 350k externally to launch my last business, and that was not easy for me to do. So to imagine the capital sums that will be wasted here for all the unforced errors made, it’s so disheartening given it was foreseeable! There are so many case studies, even from Virgin with Virgin Nigeria and Virgin America to review! James Asquith seems to be very lazy and entitled. A great opportunity not afforded to many better qualified people (not me), has been thrown away!

While I agree with everything in this article, I also feel like immediately criticizing fresh entrants and disrupters is not fair. There is not a single person in aviation that wants to see less A380’s, that want les competition transatlantic, or fewer carriers. I appreciate Global, I appreciate BOOM, and I think it is just as sensational to criticize Global as it is for them to put on a metaphorical Fyre Fest in the sky. This is responsible reporting, but let’s also at some recognize the feat that getting this particular plane in the sky, with people, to NY was. Aviation was built on the backs of visionaries and risk-takers, I hope we will continue to celebrate that spirit.

Recent findings suggest that I’m genuinely surprised that yours seems to the the only objectively credible take on this fiasco. I’ve watched a couple of the first flight review videos and the aircraft and service are laughable, yet the internet is still awash with “great to see!” and “Go Global!”, all blindly ignoring the current capabilities of the competition summarised above as if they don’t matter.

At least it’s given us a good laugh over the last few years but someone is losing money (hard to call anything sunk into this shambles an “investment”) and I imagine the flag carriers will be delighted as it makes them look stellar by comparison. Got to seriously question the judgement of anyone that wanted to get involved with Global. It’s all been smoke and mirrors from day one.

#51. Tech Report: Half Cruise, Half Cargo Ship? What It's Like to Sail French Polynesia Aboard a Local Freighter

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6 min read (1195 words)
General 🌐 Cntraveler

Tech Report: Half Cruise, Half Cargo Ship? What It's Like to Sail French Polynesia Aboard a Local Freighter

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read | Source: Cntraveler

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that it’s certainly a romantic notion to hop a freighter and sail to the distant South Pacific.
  • Sources indicate that it might come as a surprise to know that one firm has been offering dedicated cruises built around that very premise for over 40 years.
  • Fatu Hiva in the Marquesas Islands has no airport and is only accessible by sea.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it’s certainly a romantic notion to hop a freighter and sail to the distant South Pacific. One could spend days at sea staring at nothing but seabirds and cargo pallets, waking up to the sound of those pallets being offloaded onto a tiny concrete wharf, meeting a community nestled among palms. One could take the day to hike or tour the island, or feast on fresh catches with the locals, while the offloaded pallets are filled with grapefruits, dried coconut husks, and flowers to be sold elsewhere—Tahiti, perhaps.

Sources indicate that it might come as a surprise to know that one firm has been offering dedicated cruises built around that very premise for over 40 years. In French Polynesia, the locally owned cruise line Aranui Cruises offers combination passenger and cargo services from Papeete, Tahiti, to the dramatically jagged volcanic pitons and pastoral scenes of the Marquesas Islands.

Fatu Hiva in the Marquesas Islands has no airport and is only accessible by sea.

In a recent development, the idea is simple: a ship operates a cargo service to the remote islands (two of them, Fatu Hiva and Tahuata, have no airport and are only accessible by sea), and while the inbound cargo of soft drinks, groceries, building supplies, and even racing canoes is unloaded in the port, the passengers can use the time to go touring. In March 2026, I joined one such sailing, onboard the purpose-built Aranui V to see exactly what the 12-night, nearly-thousand-mile journey to the Marquesas looks like.

According to recent reports, I like to refer to the vessel as the “mullet ship”— cargo up front, cruise in the back. During the voyage, when I wasn’t swimming in the onboard pool, or enjoying a cocktail from the bar, I filled my days with lectures Dr. Carole S. Ivory, professor emerita from Washington State University, who specializes in the study of Marquesan culture and art.

Sources indicate that I got to witness that culture up close on Aranui’s included shore excursions. The experiences were visits to archaeological sites and volcanic pitons by car on Nuku Hiva, or various organized hikes on several of the other islands. There are also optional excursions for an additional fee, like the scenic drive between two sides of the island on Fatu Hiva. The drive, which traced a narrow mountain road between villages, offered spectacular vistas from the sea cliffs and, to rejoin the ship, a bonus sunset barge ride—a worthy add-on.

The Aranui V ship is a passenger cruise in the front and a cargo ship in the back.

Sources indicate that local residents hired by Aranui guide passengers in their personal cars as these tiny islands have no buses. On tiny Ua Huka, our mahu driver (a person of third-gender common in Polynesia) wearing a red flowered dress and straw hat, spent the day chatting with passengers and eating. And oh, how we ate! Baguette sandwiches during a morning stop at a craft center. A plate of chow mein from the snack bar at the botanical garden. A tour-of-the-island plate from the buffet heaped with coconut milk-roasted goat, the raw fish salad poisson cru, steamed taro, rice, and magenta-colored mashed banana swimming in sweet condensed coconut milk.

It has been revealed that on each of the islands, we passengers from the Aranui V were greeted with local musicians and artisans, typically in a community pavilion. The Marquesas are noted for their skilled carvers, working in both wood and bone to create intricately decorated bowls, decorative canoe paddles, and jewelry. Carvers also work in stone called te ke’a pua (flower stone), also known as garnet phonolite, a polished volcanic rock that has the natural appearance of being covered in crystalline flowers. The rocks themselves are found on the island of Ua Pou, and are worked into a variety of shapes: ornamental fish hooks, decorative whales and birds, and pestles used to smash taro called kea tuki popoi.

Sources indicate that unlike most cruise lines, which have multinational crews, Aranui instead runs a local cargo service that just happens to have a large international tourism component. This means all of the onboard crew are Polynesians, many of them originally from the Marquesas themselves. The service is friendly and informal, and I was often greeted on a first-name basis. A couple of the crew recognized me from my previous sailing to another island group, already some four years hence.

The passenger half of the ship has basic amenities like a pool and cocktail bar.

Aranui also doesn’t enforce the same separation between passengers and crew that is prevalent on other ships—passengers and crew can freely mingle. After dinner, many crew members and officers end up in the bar for nightcaps right alongside the passengers. On my previous voyage with Aranui, to the Austral Islands, I joined an impromptu card game in the onboard pearl boutique and watched the head of housekeeping handily clean out the ship’s captain over the course of several hands of poker, all while we and the silken strands of Tahitian Pearls in the display cases bore witness.

Sources indicate that when my only pair of sandals broke alighting from the landing craft on Ua Huka, Aranui staff directed me to the ship’s French doctor, who fixed it with tape from his medical bag. “Come back later onboard,” he noted, “and we’ll do surgery on the shoe.” While I waited, I took great amusement with a large notice on the door of the ship’s infirmary, warning that many of the fruits served onboard and in the islands have “diuretic and laxatif (sp) effect,” urging passengers to consume in moderation. I wondered how many passengers had visited the infirmary over the years with the same complaint before they felt the need to put up a sign.

Recent findings suggest that at the end of our stop on Ua Huka, we all gathered on the deck of Aranui V. We still had calls on the islands of Rangiroa and Bora Bora scheduled, but it was time to bid our goodbyes to the Marquesas in a traditional manner. A member of the onboard staff invoked a prayer of thanks for the voyage and fond farewell to these magnificent islands, which we did with armfuls of local flowers and plants cast into sunset-dappled sea to watch float ashore.

That, however, wasn’t the lasting image of the Marquesas for me. For weeks after my trip, I awoke each morning in a home that seemed suddenly foreign, recalling the smell of the straw hats, the taste of the baked banana, the green of the mountains, the red floral dress of the snacking mahu, and the pallets of coconuts and grapefruits stacked on the tiny wharf.

Editor’s Note: AirlineGeeks is proud to present our ‘Livery of the Week’ series. Every Friday, a team member will share an airline livery, which can be from the past, present, or even a special scheme. Some airline liveries are works of art. The complexity associated with painting around critical flight components and the added weight requires outside-the-box thinking from designers. The average airliner can cost upwards of $200,000 to repaint, creating a separate aircraft repainting industry as a result.

Have an idea for a livery that we should highlight? Drop us a line.

While traditional marketing theories advise airlines to avoid sponsoring events such as motor racing because of perceived associations with “danger” and “uncertainty” — concepts that could reflect negatively on air transport operators — the past couple of decades have seen several airlines establish partnerships with Formula One teams and events.

Today, some carriers are title sponsors of their home Grands Prix. Gulf Air, for example, has been the title sponsor of the Bahrain Grand Prix since its inception in 2004. Singapore Airlines, which has held the same role at the Singapore Grand Prix since 2014, has extended its commitment through 2028.

Abu Dhabi-based Etihad Airways has been the title sponsor of the UAE Grand Prix since the race’s debut in 2009. This year, it also entered into a partnership with McLaren Racing, bringing together “two organizations with a shared commitment to innovation, ambition, and delivering exceptional experiences for fans and customers around the world”.

To mark the partnership, Etihad has painted one of its Boeing 787-10 aircraft in a special livery, taking McLaren Racing’s distinctive color to the skies.

The livery features McLaren’s signature papaya orange across most of the fuselage — the same color used on its racing cars and team uniforms. The “Etihad” and “McLaren” names appear side by side above the cabin windows, while the McLaren logo is displayed toward the rear of the aircraft against a black background. The tail fin retains Etihad’s signature mosaic pattern, with its colors adjusted to complement the fuselage’s black-and-orange scheme.

Papaya has taken flight 🧡✈️Keep your eyes on the skies and let us know if you spot us 👀#McLarenF1 | #BeyondBorders | @etihad pic.twitter.com/NCHxsdAMTi.

It has been revealed that the aircraft chosen to showcase the special livery is a Boeing 787-10, registered A6-BMI. It was delivered to Etihad directly from the manufacturer on Oct. 14, 2020.

Recent findings suggest that the aircraft features one of Etihad’s older cabin designs, introduced in 2018. It has 327 seats in a two-class configuration: 32 business class seats in a 1-2-1 layout and 295 economy class seats in a 3-3-3 layout. The first 10 rows of the economy cabin are designated “Economy Space,” offering a seat pitch of 35 inches rather than the standard 31 inches.

#49. Tech Report: American Airlines Dropped One Bogus Award Fee. Alaska Airlines And Air Canada Keep Collecting Theirs.

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7 min read (1311 words)
General 🌐 Liveandletsfly

Tech Report: American Airlines Dropped One Bogus Award Fee. Alaska Airlines And Air Canada Keep Collecting Theirs.

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read | Source: Liveandletsfly

💡 Key Takeaways
  • American Airlines once charged members $75 to book an award ticket close to departure.
  • On the latest Airlines Confidential podcast, former AAdvantage chief and American Airlines Chief Information Officer Maya Leibman discussed an airline fee she had trouble defending, as flagged by View From The Wing.
  • In a recent development, american continued collecting its close-in award booking fee after the ticketing process became automated.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

American Airlines once charged members $75 to book an award ticket close to departure. The airline eventually eliminated that fee, but a newly introduced account from its former loyalty chief offers a revealing reminder: the work used to justify a charge can disappear long before the charge does.

On the latest Airlines Confidential podcast, former AAdvantage chief and American Airlines Chief Information Officer Maya Leibman discussed an airline fee she had trouble defending, as flagged by View From The Wing.

In a recent development, american continued collecting its close-in award booking fee after the ticketing process became automated. Members without an applicable elite waiver paid $75 when booking within 21 days of departure. Leibman recalled that “we were still charging an expedite fee, like, within 21 days,” even though the transaction was “all done automatically.”.

In a recent development, american eliminated the fee in January 2020. Like Gary, I appreciate hearing a former executive acknowledge the tension with collecting money for an expedited process that no longer required anyone to expedite it. I would rather hear that candid admission than a strained argument trying to justify it.

It has been revealed that I can also understand why manually processing an award ticket once required time and resources and understand why an airline might have charged more to complete that work shortly before departure. But when a computer concerns the ticket, what exactly is being expedited?

Recent findings suggest that the airline still has expenses, of course. Maintaining a reservation system costs money. So does operating a loyalty program. But those expenses also exist when someone books a ticket three months before departure and do not explain why an otherwise identical automated transaction should suddenly cost another $75 inside a 21-day window.

The more straightforward explanation is that American could collect the money, so it did.

It has been revealed that airlines do not price everything according to the cost of providing it, and I do not expect them to. A last-minute seat may command a premium because demand supports it. But if that is the rationale, call it a premium for booking at the last minute. Calling it a processing expense just makes frequent flyers jaded. And whatever you call it, customers are understandably going to hate it because it does not correlate to any legitimate expense unless you count the sunk cost of the investment in the automation system.

American dropped its fee, but I see the same problem today with partner award booking fees at Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards and Air Canada Aeroplan.

It has been revealed that I covered the Atmos fee increase earlier this year. Aeroplan also spells out its charge in its flight reward policy and makes it clear when booking online or on the Air Canada app.

These are airline-imposed charges, of course, not government taxes, though they are often lumped into the same section to suggest that you’re paying taxes, not fees. Here, you can do the searching, select the flights, enter your information, and complete an ordinary booking online, yet still pay extra for the privilege of redeeming your points on a partner.

I consider these bogus fees. They are revenue-generating measures, and I will not defend them as some necessary surcharge for the work involved in issuing my ticket. But by bogus that doesn’t mean that I fail to understand why they are levied.

Industry observers note that yes, programs pay partner airlines for award travel, bu that is part of offering partner awards in the first place. It should already inform the economics of selling points and setting redemption prices. Collecting another cash charge from the member is a commercial choice.

For my family of four, the Atmos fee alone adds $160 to a round-trip partner award unless a waiver applies (and I don’t have the credit card right now). That is real money, especially when we are already redeeming a substantial number of points.

There is one concession I will make: these fees are published and displayed during booking. We can account for them when deciding what the points and the program are worth.

If an award costs 50,000 points plus taxes and a partner booking fee, that cash payment belongs in my valuation. I should not calculate the value of the redemption as though the fee does not exist.

A program with an annoying booking fee can still offer a better overall deal than a program without one. I would happily pay $20 to save thousands of points on an otherwise comparable itinerary. But that makes the redemption worthwhile despite the fee. It does not make the fee itself worthwhile.

The same applies when earning or buying points. If I expect to redeem primarily on partners, those charges reduce what I am willing to pay for the currency. Transparency lets us make that calculation, so at least there is that.

American Airlines deserves credit for eventually eliminating its $75 close-in award booking fee. Leibman’s recollection helps explain why members were right to question it: the process became automated, but the charge remained.

Partner award booking fees at Atmos Rewards and Aeroplan strike me as similarly unappealing revenue measures. I still use both programs, and a good redemption can easily outweigh the extra cash required. But I bake those charges into my valuation rather than pretend they are justified by some special service I am receiving.

Sometimes a fee survives because collecting it is profitable, which his hardly breaking news, but something I appreciate Leibman confirming explicitly.

Beond Airlines Suspends Flights Again: Will They Resume In December?

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read | Source: Onemileatatime

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Back in April 2026, we saw Beond Airlines suspend all scheduled operations for the summer, as the airline claimed it would resume flights as of October.
  • According to recent reports, beond Airlines launched operations in 2023, and it brands itself as the world’s first premium leisure airline.
  • Anyway, in mid-April 2026, the company announced that it would suspend its scheduled operations for the entire summer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Back in April 2026, we saw Beond Airlines suspend all scheduled operations for the summer, as the airline claimed it would resume flights as of October. Then in October, it unveiled it would return in December. Is that actually happening now, or what exactly is going on?

According to recent reports, beond Airlines launched operations in 2023, and it brands itself as the world’s first premium leisure airline. The manufacturer is headquartered in Dubai, but primarily operates flights to and from the Maldives. I reviewed the airline in 2024, and the onboard product was super pleasant. The airline right now has a fleet of two aircraft, including one A319 and one A321.

Anyway, in mid-April 2026, the company announced that it would suspend its scheduled operations for the entire summer. The airline promised to resume flights in October, for the winter season.

Sources indicate that then in October, the airline confirmed that it would suspend operations through November 30, 2026, meaning it will resume flights as of December 1, 2026. Interestingly, the airline has promised to provide a schedule update by November 12, 2026, but that date has now come and gone, and there was no update.

So I guess it remains to be seen if we actually see a resumption of flights as of December, or if the timeline will get pushed back again. The company does have a section on its travel updates page with FAQs, and one of the questions is “will the dates change again?” The answer is “we chose dates we are confident in,” but also notes that “if anything changes, you will hear from us first.”.

Sources indicate that beond Airlines does have its “commitment” to customers when looks change, which includes the ability to change destinations or travel dates, receive a travel credit valid for 18 months, or to receive a full refund. A change of destinations or dates, plus a travel credit, isn’t worth a whole lot for an airline that keeps pushing back its relaunch.

Sources indicate that interestingly, but perhaps not surprisingly, earlier this year the airline deleted its customer promise webpage, which used to guarantee rebooking on another airline in business class in the event a flight is canceled, or else the airline would offer a free flight. That page is now gone, and there’s no mention of rebooking on another airline.

So the airline will “support you every step of the way,” unless you actually want to take the vacation you booked, in which case you’re out of luck (which is less than ideal, given that many Maldives properties have very strict cancelation policies).

While Beond Airlines’ business blueprint was questionable under the best of circumstances, the crisis of this year makes matters worse:.

So I feel bad for Beond, and I’m not trying to do a “told you so, I was right” thing, because these are of course exceptional circumstances. The thing that made me suspicious about Beond for so long is that the airline would repeatedly make outlandish growth announcements, only to rarely follow through on them. That’s neither here nor there, though.

Keep in mind that since operations were initially suspended in April, we’ve seen some interesting developments:.

My assumption is that Saudi Arabia is to some extent funding the Red Sea flights, given how the country is throwing money at any airline willing to fly there. However, one wonders if that’s enough money to make the math work, or if Beond even has the general funding right now to keep things operating.

It’s just all so strange, because it feels like half of the announcements from Beond Airlines are really targeting prospective investors, constantly promoting how it’s going to open new subsidiaries all over the world, launch dozens of new routes, etc.

According to recent reports, as I said in April, I didn’t think it was a sure bet that flights would resume in October. Now we’ll see if flights actually resume in December.

Sources indicate that in the spring of 2026, all-business class airline Beond suspended scheduled operations through October 2026. That timeline has come and gone, and now the airline claims it’ll resume operations as of December 2026. Over the summer, we learned that the airline wasn’t paying many staff for months, and the airline is now pivoting to operating service via Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea Airport.

Recent findings suggest that we’ll see what happens in the coming weeks. Presumably the Red Sea service gets the airline some money from the Saudi government, but it remains to be seen if that’s enough to keep this operation afloat.

It’s understandable that the current situation is really challenging, between the price of jet fuel, plus overall sentiment about the Middle East. However, I have to imagine the airline didn’t have great financial health before this whole mess started, and suspending flights in some ways only makes things even worse.

How do you see this playing out for Beond?

#47. Virgin Atlantic Ups The Ante In India, As The World Dials In

Virgin Atlantic Ups The Ante In India, As The World Dials In

📅 03 Jun 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Source: Godsavethepoints

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that this week, Virgin Atlantic celebrates 25 years of flying to India.
  • On the sidelines of the IATA Annual General Meeting, basically the UN General Assembly of airlines, the newly introduced strategic partnership for India was unveiled with very interesting nods to the future.
  • IndiGo carries more passengers in India than anyone else and will connect US and UK/European customers flying Virgin, Delta and Air France KLM onward in India, while also helping fill seats for these European and North American partners, as their own customers head West.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that this week, Virgin Atlantic celebrates 25 years of flying to India. In Virgin fashion, it’s doing so in style, with a joint announcement among partners Delta Airlines, Air France-KLM, and a latest strategic partner IndiGo.

On the sidelines of the IATA Annual General Meeting, basically the UN General Assembly of airlines, the newly introduced strategic partnership for India was unveiled with very interesting nods to the future.

IndiGo carries more passengers in India than anyone else and will connect US and UK/European customers flying Virgin, Delta and Air France KLM onward in India, while also helping fill seats for these European and North American partners, as their own customers head West.

That’s probably a good thing, because with recent service additions, Virgin now flies a million seats a year to India and it sounds like others are piling on more flights too. It’s now one of the largest operators to India.

Sources indicate that I’ve been bullish on India as the next great center of the world for a while now. It’s not necessarily that I’m at all intelligent, it’s just based on the fact that India is the world’s largest population. But, when Ed Bastian, Delta’s formidable CEO says it, people tend to listen. Bastian mentioned India being the most important aviation market globally now and signaled a return of direct services for the carrier as well.

Virgin has been a small step ahead, adding service regularly on their Delhi, Mumbai and Bangalore routes. IndiGo chose this alliance over formidable competition and this will certainly be a space to watch as more global airlines and alliances focus on India.

Geo-political activity points to India becoming a latest manufacturing super power, in addition to its prolific work in tech, IT and customer service, not to mention blossoming tourism. These kind of globally connected businesses are massive business, huge in fact, for corporate contracts and easy onward connectivity to regional sites is essential. The partnership makes sense.

Recent findings suggest that in a somewhat rare and impressive signal of unity and seriousness towards India, Virgin Atlantic made their India crews part of the core Virgin family, rather than as contractors through a third party local manufacturer, known in aviation world as a GSA. This means Virgin’s India crews are a part of the full team, with benefits too.

When asked about loyalty implications of the latest alliance, Virgin Atlantic CEO, Shai Weiss, noted a mutual passion for using loyalty to enhance guest experience far beyond just the earn and burn of points and miles. For future iterations, they’ve offered the following….

The MoU (memorandum of understanding) also creates a framework for deeper collaboration between the carriers on a bilateral and multilateral basis; contemplates commercial collaboration including network, loyalty, cargo and sales, subject to regulatory approvals; explores areas of non-commercial cooperation including aircraft maintenance, sustainability, training, ground handling; and acknowledges the need to develop advanced collaboration through use of technology to efficiently service joint customers.

IndiGo will provide onward connectivity for Virgin and the other strategic partners to 32 destinations, making it easier than ever to see Udaipur, Jaipur, Mumbai, Kashmir and delights further south in Bangalore and Goa.

I just returned from the lovely Leela Palace in Delhi, as I watched the news happen live.

To me, India is a country of joy. Even people with truly nothing seem to find positivity and it’s generally a way of life here. Hospitality is as warm and steeped in tradition as it comes, too. It’s hot, it’s humid, but it’s an experience unlike any other and that’s something that’s harder to say these days than I’d like.

The food, ugh. I adore. Sure, I’ll take a dosa from the South over a heavy curry from the North most days, but I love both and if you don’t love a good black daahl there’s something wrong with you.

Sources indicate that in short, it’s already fairly easy to get to India but it’s about to get a whole lot easier and not just to hub cities too. More seats means more chances to use points, by the way!

We didn’t have to wait long to find out how American Airlines is shaking up its route map in Los Angeles.

Recent findings suggest that just minutes after TPG reported the carrier was planning a route announcement at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), American revealed its looks. And there’s both good and bad news for AA flyers in Southern California.

Most notably, the carrier intends to bolster its service on four routes to major U.S. cities.

It’s also bringing back a route to Colorado that it hasn’t offered in a half-decade.

Plus, American will end service to two cities from LAX.

All told, Friday's changes cover nine routes from its West Coast hub. Here's what to know.

American confirmed it’s bringing back service to Grand Junction, Colorado, for the first time in five years.

Recent findings suggest that it will operate seasonal regional service from LAX between May 27 and Aug. 9 with a Bombardier CRJ700.

American last operated LAX service to Grand Junction Regional Airport (GJT) in 2021, according to data from aviation analytics firm Cirium.

In 2027, this route will effectively replace American’s flight to Colorado’s Aspen/Pitkin County Airport (ASE), which will be closed next summer for construction.

American will fly its LAX-GJT route with one of its smaller CRJ-700 aircraft.

Elsewhere, American will turn to two routes it’s previously offered seasonally — and sporadically —from LAX into more regular service:.

Both routes will operate with an Embraer 175 regional jet.

According to recent reports, starting next spring, American will also add extra daily flights from LAX to several major U.S. cities.

In a recent development, denver, Las Vegas and Seattle will all get additional frequencies. Plus, American will double its daily service on one transcontinental route — from LA to Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD).

Starting in May, American will offer twice-daily Dulles service. That’ll make the IAD-LAX routes a stronger complement to AA’s cross-country Los Angeles service from nearby Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA).

American will cut ties with its LAX route to Cleveland Hopkins International Airport (CLE) effective Feb. 11.

That same day, it will also end service to Des Moines, Iowa.

This network revamp in LA comes a day after American executives remarked the carrier was rethinking the routes it offers at its Southern California hub.

American’s LAX service today sharply lags the flight offerings it had at the airport in 2019.

Industry observers note that speaking Thursday, American’s chief commercial officer, Nat Pieper, said the airline would aim to offer more flights from LAX to major U.S. cities in a push to win more L.A.-based flyers.

"We’re going to grow and we’re going to invest in the local market,” he said, speaking Thursday at the Skift Aviation Forum in Upcoming York.

That expansion, Pieper noted, will be gradual — and ramp up — as infrastructure work at LAX progresses over the next two years.

  • Boeing admits the 737 MAX 9 whose door plug blew out on Alaska Airlines flight 1282 “was not reasonably safe in construction” when it left the factory.
